utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is open. Please call the case, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Tuesday, the 6th of March, 2012. Let me greet everybody in the courtroom. I'll give the floor to Ms. Biersay without further ado, who's going to continue with her arguments on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor and will say some more about Exhibit 1200.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yesterday before I concluded I was describing to the Trial Chamber the series of SRS press conferences that the accused gave during this period of May and June of 1992, and specifically in and around the time that non-Serbs were being tortured and murdered at the Ekonomija farm and Ciglane factory in Zvornik. Now, yesterday I talked about a rally that was given by the accused and other members of the SRS, and that rally was published on the 28th of May, 1992, and according to the report it said "yesterday." So the rally happened exactly before these crimes were being committed. Now, I don't know what Mr. Seselj is talking about. And if he has something to say on this issue, it should wait until he has his ten hours to use. So not only were non-Serbs being killed around the time of that May 27th, 1992, rally; they're also being killed by Seseljevci around the time of other press conferences, like the ones in May -- at the end of May, 1992, around the same time that a group of Seseljevci murdered 88 non-Serbs at the Drinjaca Dom Kulture in Zvornik. And again, when he gave a press conference on June 4th, this is around the same time that a group led by Seselj's Vojvoda Vidovic murdered 22 non-Serb men and women in Ljesevo, Ilijas. And when he gave the other one in June -- on June 11th, 1992, that's around the same time that 740 non-Serbs were being massacred in Karakaj and Gero's slaughter-house. Poisoned by the accused's persecution propaganda, the accused's Seseljevci and other forces were unleashed to the epicentre of ethnic conflict and violence. In the crime bases where his volunteers were in the field of operations, Serb forces committed crimes. Now, to be clear, his Seseljevci need not be physical perpetrators for him to be found guilty of the crimes charged; it is not required. However, crimes were often committed by volunteers associated with the accused and he honoured these perpetrators again and again. And to some of them, he gave the very special title that he himself had, that of Vojvoda. He filled his Vojvodas, he filled his Seseljevci, and he filled Serb forces with his hateful propaganda, which they took with them to the front lines. His ability to offer a fighting force was a significant contribution to the common purpose of the JCE and it was a substantial contribution to the commission of the charged crimes. He had the influence, he had the authority to promise practical assistance to Serb forces throughout the former Yugoslavia. And as Mr. Marcussen explained, consequently, because of this ability, other JCE members - suffering from manpower shortages - appealed to him for volunteers. And that set forth in Exhibits P226, P652, and P239, for example. The accused promised and delivered volunteers to Eastern Slavonia, including Vukovar; to the Krajina; to Western Slavonia; and throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. That he could both make and keep such promises undermines any claim by him that he was a political figure disconnected from military organisation and operations. His persecution propaganda served to facilitate his contribution of manpower. His inflammatory public statements were used to recruit volunteers. His visits to the front lines strengthened their indoctrination and were used to reinforce the branding of non-Serbs as threats to be removed. In one -- and the Trial Chamber should take in account, this is a public speech that he gives to his Seseljevci. And by "public," I mean it's being televised, that he gives to his Seseljevci before sending them to the Vukovar front lines. And in a minute I'll ask that P17 be played. Now, in this clip the accused called the volunteers going to Vukovar, he called them Serb Chetnik heros and emphasised that they were fighting in an ethnically Serb army and for Serbian land. And at this time I'd ask that P17 be played.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Reporter: ... is the common struggle together with the Yugoslav People's Army for the final liberation of Vukovar. To the question if the volunteers would be sent to Grubisno Polje, one of the deputies of the volunteer detachment replied that Vukovar had priority over other regions. Here is what Branko Vasiljevic told us. "Reporter: How old are you? "BV: 58. "Reporter: Where are you from? "BV: Nis born and bred. "Reporter: And where are you going? "BV: I'm going to help the brothers ... "Reporter: Are you alone? "BV: ... brothers in arms. No, I have two sons. "Reporter: Are they here too? "BV: They came 10 to 15 days ago. One is in Borovo and the other one in Knin. My uncle was a commander, so blood is thicker than water. "Reporter: Mr. Seselj held a speech in front of a group of volunteers standing in line and said the following on that occasion. "Seselj: God bless you heros! "Volunteers: God bless you too! "Seselj: Brothers Serbs, Serb Chetnik heros, you are going to the war today! "Today you are going to liberate the Serbian Vukovar and defend the Serbian Slavonia. You are going to join hundreds of thousands of our volunteers. You are leaving from all parts of today's reduced Serbia to restore the glory of the Serbian arms. You will co-operate with the Yugoslav army units, since this is our army. Most of all, it is the Serbian army, considering the ethnicity of its officers and its struggle for the salvation of the Serbian country and Serbian territories. "Reporter: Mr. Seselj finished with the words: 'Good luck, guys. See you in Vukovar.' Do these words mean that he too will join the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party is yet to be seen."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Many of the Seseljevci units established, recruited, and organised by the accused participated both during 1991 in combat operations to seize and cleanse parts of Croatia as well as parts of BiH in 1992. The Seseljevci were deployed to vital and difficult areas. The scope of the accused's volunteer recruitment and deployment was vast. It was vast in terms of the significant numbers of volunteers mobilised to the front line, in terms of the geographic area they covered, and in terms of their notoriety for brutality against non-Serbs. Now, Your Honours, I have -- we have prepared a slide illustrating some of the places to which the Seseljevci were deployed. And at this time I'd ask that the slide be displayed. And it's based on a number of sources and I'd be happy to provide those separately to the Trial Chamber, but the core of it, it's based on the P217, P218, and the statements by and evidence of the former SRS senior members as well as other evidence. And you can see that -- and as the Trial Chamber is well aware, the Seseljevci were deployed throughout the crime-base areas and the pattern municipalities. So you see them clustered around Vukovar. They're also in and around Vocin, Zvornik, Greater Sarajevo, and Herzegovina, where Mostar and Nevesinje are located, Bijeljina, Bosanski Samac, and other places like the Krajina, which is in the -- on the western side of that slide, which can be removed at this time. The accused himself, in Exhibit P342, has put the number of Seseljevci as high as almost 30.000 and he admitted that he contributed around 10.000 volunteers to the common purpose in BiH alone. As early as May 1991 - and this date -- that date, that's around the time that the Seseljevci participated in the killing of Croat police officers in Borovo Selo. Around that time according to -- according to P1275, there were already 15.000 Chetniks in the accused's ranks. Between January and July of 1992, more than 6.000 Seseljevci were stationed and trained at barracks in Belgrade before being deployed to the front. Vojvoda Branislav Gavrilovic, aka Brne, and I'll discuss him a little bit more shortly, he established volunteer training centres in Greater Sarajevo through which at least 1500 Seseljevci passed during the course of the war. And that's just one small area. The evidence, including Exhibits C10, P1275, P54, and P1000, has proven beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused made a significant contribution of thousands of Seseljevci to facilitate the crimes charged in the indictment. And I'd also refer the Trial Chamber to P1219. Now, this was a massive organisation, and so the accused had machinery in place to handle that. And his SRS and SCP Crisis Staff and war staffs were created to spear-head his deployment of volunteers. Senior members of the SRS war staff recounted that as leader of both the SRS and the Serbian Chetnik Movement, the accused made all important decisions concerning their policies and operations. The accused appointed Witness Petkovic as head of the War Staff and Rankic was the deputy head. And their admitted statements, for example, P1074, P1076, and C11, describe how the accused maintained complete power over the Crisis and War Staffs. Witness Rankic, for example, noted that: "Seselj had absolute power and made all the decisions himself." One of the functions of the SRS War Staff was to co-ordinate arming and training of the Seseljevci with other JCE members. And again, high-ranking members of the SRS War Staff, like Rankic and Petkovic, visited training camps to arrange for the arrival and deployment of volunteers. The accused also visited and inspected volunteers at training centres, and that has been mentioned by Mr. Marcussen. He highlighted Exhibit P528, in which the accused addressed volunteers at the Erdut training centre, telling them that Serb Chetniks had laid down their lives in the defence of Borovo Selo. He also told volunteers that wherever there were Ustasha, they should be killed and expelled because it was all Serbian territory. The accused gave similar orders to volunteers in private, and, for example - I'm not going to say the name of the witness. I will cite the exhibits pertaining to the witness - he directed one volunteer to cleanse everything in a particular area and "to kill Muslim civilians without mercy ..." And that's described in Exhibits P1129, pages 218 to 219; P1128, at page 2; and P1112, at page 11. And they have to be read together as the Trial Chamber will understand. The evidence beyond a reasonable doubt shows that the accused was more than a recruiter of volunteers for the JNA. This quasi-military politician exercised his authority and influence over each and every aspect related to the volunteers, even though he did not have operational command over them. He decided where his volunteers were deployed and he deployed them in units, so not on an individual volunteer-by-volunteer basis. Discrete units identified as Seseljevci. Unit commanders were appointed by the accused or the SRS War Staff that he controlled. And this is shown, for example, in Exhibit P227, which was sent by a member of the War Staff to a TO and required that the TO "co-ordinate with our unit command" as a condition of sending the volunteers. So we will send you volunteers, but you must co-ordinate with our unit command in order for that to happen. Witness Petkovic, in Exhibit C18, explained that the War Staff decided to send a unit, for example, under Vojvoda Debeli's command to Bosanski Samac in spring 1992. And it was the accused himself who chose the commanders of that unit. And more specifically, I'd refer the Trial Chamber to paragraphs 49, 53, and 56. The accused personally approved the sending of volunteers for the operations in Zvornik and Mostar. Petkovic described how the War Staff supervised local Crisis Staffs, SRS boards, and commanders, but "there was only one leader, and that was Seselj." Once in the field, the accused's volunteers were generally subordinated to the local TO, to the JNA, or VRS, or MUP units, but the accused received regular reports about field activities, both through the War Staff and through direct reporting by his commanders at the front lines. They telephoned him. They visited the Belgrade SRS/SCP office to meet him in person. And as a result of those close contacts, he could and he did intervene in field operations as he deemed necessary. And I would refer the Trial Chamber to, for example, Exhibit P59; P688, at paragraph 50; Exhibit P1074, at page 49; and Exhibit P1058, at paragraph 21. Witness Glamocanin, in Exhibit P688, described the accused as having "command and control" over volunteers in the field. The SRS War Staff had the authority to issue orders to its units in the field regarding, for example, where the units would be deployed and when they should be withdrawn. I would refer the Trial Chamber to Exhibit P221. Witness Rankic, again in Exhibit P1074, confirmed that regrouping and redeployment orders were given by the SRS War Staff to an SRS commander in Vocin. Likewise, Seseljevci of the Kragujevac Chetnik detachment, they were ordered by Rankic to participate in a joint operation to forcibly take over targeted villages in Croatia. And again, I'd refer the Trial Chamber to Exhibit P253; P225; and C11, page 12. The accused also had the power and influence to intervene personally to assist his volunteers in the field. For example, as shown by intercept Exhibits P513 and 514, one of which I'll play in a moment, when the accused wanted to have a group of his volunteers commanded by Vojvoda Gavrilovic rescued from an ambush in and around Sarajevo in April 1992, he threatened Serb political and military leadership in BiH that if they weren't pulled out, he would withdraw all his men from the front lines and "never deploy them again." And so at this time I'd ask that Exhibit P513 be played, and it's an intercept so it's not a video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Seselj: This is Vojislav Seselj. Could I speak to Branislav Gavrilovic? "Unknown male person: Yes, sir. One moment, please. "Gavrilovic: God bless you, Vojvoda. "Seselj: God bless you. What's going on there? "Gavrilovic: Well, Vojo, our men are down there in the town, you know. "Seselj: How many of them? "Gavrilovic: 18. 18 are left. "Seselj: Are they surrounded? "Gavrilovic: Sorry? "Seselj: Are they surrounded? "Gavrilovic: They've been surrounded since the beginning. The volunteers have left down there to get them out and we don't know about anything happening down there. "Seselj: You're wounded, right? "Gavrilovic: Yes, in my leg. "Seselj: What's the wound like? "Gavrilovic: Well, the bullet went through but I'll be all right. There won't be any problems. "Seselj: Have you been given any medical attention? "Gavrilovic: Yes, yes, everything's fine. "Seselj: Look, I've just called Pale. I can't find Radovan and nobody can find him. "Gavrilovic: Yes. "Seselj: But I've left a message that if they don't get our men out, we'll withdraw all our men from the front lines and we'll never deploy them again. "Gavrilovic: All right. "Seselj: You know. Please don't lose your nerves ... "Gavrilovic: The people ... "Seselj: ... don't get into arguments with your men offhand. Only try to find as many men as possible to get these out, you know. "Gavrilovic: Well, they're constantly being deployed to get them out all the time. "Seselj: We'll clean these things up when it's more peaceful. "Gavrilovic: All right, Vojo. How's your health? "Seselj: It's not bad. Please try and have as many people sent over here as possible. "Gavrilovic: Well, all right. Everyone's active and sending people down there. We'll see, something will come out of this. "Seselj: All right. "Gavrilovic: Right, cheers ... "Seselj: Do you have this number here? "Gavrilovic: I do, I do. "Seselj: Well, all right. Please let me know then. I can barely get through here. I have been calling this number for over an hour. I can barely get through. "Gavrilovic: All right. "Seselj: It's probably easier for you because not everybody's calling this number. "Gavrilovic: All right. All right. "Seselj: So please let me know what's going on. "Gavrilovic: I'll let you know. Cheers. "Seselj: Hang in there."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And of course his men were rescued and in intercept P514, which I won't play, Momcilo Mandic recognises and acknowledges that Seselj has just called from Belgrade. And he gave -- he passed on the information that that group should be pulled out and they were. And all of this illustrates the accused's power to direct volunteers on the front line and to enforce his will with other JCE members. This was not a recruiting sergeant or agent for the JNA. He was much more. He knew where his Seseljevci were deployed. He received information from the front lines. He communicated with them. He communicated with other leaders of the Serb forces. And he decided when, where, and how his Seseljevci worked with other Serb forces. In other words, the accused was not recruiting and deploying volunteers at arm's length. He was intimately involved in every aspect of inspiring them to his cause and deploying them to commit crimes. On the 13th of May, 1993, reflected in P1219, the accused held a press conference to announce his promotion of Vojvodas, a ceremony held as war raged in BiH. And the Trial Chamber previously saw that at the beginning of the presentation as video P255. The accused continued to hold large-scale rallies and celebrations of Chetniks to evoke their bloody past and their crimes against non-Serbs, including Muslims. The evidence shows he publicly promoted men who committed crimes throughout the former Yugoslavia. Now, I'd like to show the Trial Chamber - and if we could please show it now - a slide listing the Seseljevci who were promoted to Vojvoda by the accused because you will hear some of the names again. And this is just to give you a little context for those names when they pop up. In Vukovar, Milan Lancuzanin, aka Kameni; Miroslav Vukovic, also at Vukovar, aka Cele; Branislav Gavrilovic, aka Brne; Branislav Vakic. In Bijeljina and Brcko, Mirko Blagojevic. In Bosanski Samac, Srecko Radovanovic, aka Debeli. In Zvornik, Miroslav Vukovic, aka Cele. In Greater Sarajevo, Vasilije Vidovic, aka Vaske; Slavko Aleksic; Branislav Gavrilovic, aka Brne; and Nikola Poplasen. Now, as the Trial Chamber has heard, there are repetitions of certain names and he redeployed them from one crime base to the next. Wherever Seseljevci went, crimes were committed. Wherever Vojvodas went, crimes were committed. Often it was the Seseljevci committing those crimes, the Vojvodas committing those crimes. And from the very start of his persecution campaign, the accused was well aware that his impact through his contributions was, indeed, significant and substantial. He describes in Exhibit P1180 how it showed how successful the Serbian Chetnik Movement was because Croats and Muslims sometimes weren't sleeping in their houses because they heard that the Chetniks were coming. But Biljana Plavsic really described the core of the accused's impact. He motivated Serb fighters and he frightened non-Serbs, and she said in Exhibit P1310: "He came to see us, visited the front; his presence meant a lot to the men. The troops would talk about his visits long after he would leave. On the other hand, news that he was at the front would act as a great demoralising factor for our enemies." He knew the impact he had. He knew it from the thousands of volunteers he successfully raised and deployed to implement the common criminal purpose. He knew it from the crowd responses at his rallies. He knew, and that is why he never stopped using his hate propaganda as a weapon and why he has not even stopped today. Through his hate propaganda, the accused relentlessly promoted the forcible establishment of ethnically Serb territories encompassing significant parts of Croatia and BiH. He inspired fear and hatred in Serbs that non-Serbs were their enemies. He then used this fear and hatred of non-Serbs to create and to aggravate an atmosphere conducive to violent acts against targeted non-Serbs. Through his campaign of recruitment, organisation, and deployment of volunteers, he assisted the other Serb forces in their fight for the creation of separate Serb-dominated territories in Croatia and later in BiH, all the time co-ordinating the activities of Seseljevci with other JCE members. He encouraged and instigated groups and individuals within the Serb forces, including Seseljevci. And this has been proven beyond a reasonable doubt and the time has come for him to be held accountable for his crimes. In conclusion, the accused cannot suppress the evidence, and that evidence shows that his Seseljevci and Serb forces worked together to commit the crimes charged in the indictment. And ethnic cleansing was accomplished by using the same tactics again and again and again. Non-Serb villages were shelled and destroyed. Areas seen as rightfully Serb were forcibly taken over by Serb forces. Non-Serb families were ripped apart as children and men -- as children and women were isolated from men, rounded up and either sent to camps where they were abused, raped, and killed, or were forced to flee for their own safety. And non-Serbs were prevented, by fear or force, from returning to their homes, many of which - along with their religious and cultural sites - had been plundered or destroyed. That is what the evidence shows. At this time, Your Honour, I will turn the lectern over to my colleague Ms. Hochhauser, and she will describe how these tactics were replicated in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Hochhauser. You have the floor. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and good morning. Before the conflict began, the people of Vukovar municipality in Croatia lived in a prosperous, generally peaceful multi-ethnic community. By November 21st of 1991, those same citizens of Vukovar were intractably divided by ethnic hatred. They had lost loved ones, their homes, and their city to shelling and violence aimed at driving them out of Vukovar. The crimes committed in Vukovar municipality were committed in furtherance of the common purpose of the joint criminal enterprise and the Serb forces - the JNA, the local TOs, and volunteers, including Seseljevci - were the perpetrators of those crimes. Just as they had throughout other targeted areas of Croatia, beginning in August 1991, and just as they would go on to do in targeted areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Serb forces wreaked havoc on the lives of the people of Vukovar in pursuit of their common goal of an ethnically homogenous Serb nation. The accused, along with the other political and military leaders that were members of the joint criminal enterprise charged in this case, saw Vukovar as strategically important to the achievement of their common goal. The accused spoke of Vukovar's exceptional significance to Serbia and the Serbian people, calling it, in P1208 at page 10, "equally Serbian" as Belgrade. The accused characterised the battle for Vukovar in discriminatory terms, describing the municipality as "the most powerful Ustasha stronghold" upon which Serb victory would depend. As shown here in a clip from P298.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "J: How significant is the liberation of Vukovar for Serbia and the Serbian people? "S: It is of exceptional significance, exceptional. This is the most powerful of Ustasha strongholds. Once Vukovar is taken, Ustashas have no chance of saving either Osijek or Vinkovci. There is nothing to stop our forces. Vukovar is the key line that needs to be broken through, that needs to be captured, and ... that if Vukovar falls here, if Slunj falls in Serbian Krajina, then Tudjman's Ustasha regime in Zagreb will fall too. And that is why this battle is decisive."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: The JCE's persecutory campaign in Vukovar was clear. As JNA General Panic said, in Exhibit P261 at page 219, Vukovar would be "a Serb enclave," or in the words of the accused, at P1186, page 6, "that town will be the capital of Serbian Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem." And added: "The Serb people have to return there." Indeed, as discussed earlier by Mr. Marcussen, the SAO SBWS had already been created in June 1991 and a government led by JCE member Goran Hadzic had been formed in August and September 1991. So to implement their common purpose in Vukovar, the JCE members sent Serb forces and structures controlled by them in large numbers and those forces and structures supported one another. The largest part of Vukovar, including the areas of Ovcara and Grabovo, were situated within the zone of responsibility of the JNA's Operational Group South. The importance of Vukovar to the common purpose of the JCE was further reflected by JCE member Adzic's order, assigning the JNA elite Guards Motorised Brigade to Vukovar on 30 September 1991. The Guards Motorised Brigade was a premier unit of the JNA. Its personnel were carefully selected, they were highly trained, and they were well equipped. And after 7 October 1991, it was under the command of Mile Mrksic. On 10 October 1991, the Assembly of the SAO SBWS, led again by Goran Hadzic, attached the local Serb TO officially to the JNA. The Seseljevci didn't arrive in Vukovar of their own accord. The Vukovar TO sent a request for volunteers to the SRS War Staff, and it was the accused who decided that the unit which would go on to be called the Leva Supoderica Detachment, which I will refer to, Your Honours, as LSD, to Vukovar in response to that request. The LSD arrived in Vukovar in early October, and it was primarily composed of Seseljevci, many of whom were natives of the area, including Milan Lancuzanin, aka Kameni, commander of the LSD and later a Vojvoda. Other fighters in the detachment were recruited elsewhere by the SRS War Staff. And as expert Theunens and Witness VS-012 both discussed, those Seseljevci - sent from elsewhere - were equipped and trained in association with MUP Serbia, under the authority of JCE members Stanisic and Simatovic, and often in co-operation with JCE member Arkan, as well as by the JNA, under the authority of JCE members Kadijevic and Adzic. P250, signed in Sid on 18 October 1991, demonstrated unequivocally that the TO recognised and incorporated the LSD under the command of Kameni. P199, the decision on the continuation of the assault operation on Vukovar, signed by Mile Mrksic on 29 October, specifically identifies the LSD as being under the command of Mrksic and the JNA. And the JNA on the ground in Vukovar took pride in the seamless co-ordination and integration into the JNA of the TO and volunteers, as can be seen in the clip of this interview with Major Sljivancanin of the JNA in Vukovar. And I'd ask now that P291 please be played.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Major, could you please describe briefly today's combat activities here in this area. "VS: Well, all the units in the territory of Vukovar are fighting under the unified command of the 'South' Operations Group and command of the Yugoslav People's Army, which is very important. Volunteers often say: 'You never mention us,' and then I think we're all of the same kind and we fight under the same command ... everyone, whoever comes ... we equip them right away, prepare them for combat, and include them in the units of the JNA. They carry out combat activities side by side with other soldiers. The enemy, that is, the Ustashas, are completely defeated ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: The accused was actively and intimately involved in the events in Vukovar and with the actions of his Seseljevci once they arrived there. Vojvoda Branislav Vakic and Vojvoda Branislav Gavrilovic, aka Brne, were also sent to Vukovar with Seseljevci units. And the accused appointed Slobodan Katic, an experienced fighter from Belgrade, as the leader of the Seseljevci who were sent from Belgrade and subordinated him and his unit to the LSD, which, of course, was in turn subordinated to the local TO. Witnesses Petkovic and Rankic both stated that the accused kept in close contact with Kameni and communicated with him directly, as with his other commanders in Vukovar. According to Witness Petkovic, both Katic and Kameni treated Seselj -- treated the accused, excuse me, as their commander. And they both went to SRS headquarters regularly to speak with him. At the time of the conflict, the accused also took great pride in the lock-step co-ordination between his men in Vukovar and the JNA and TO, and he boasted of the Seseljevci's significant contribution to the achievements of the Serb fighting force there. And I'd ask you now to play, as we can see in P185.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We painted almost all the helmets over. Wait a second! One of those army helmets ... you know what, guys, I am used to everybody being silent while I am talking. Perhaps you still haven't developed this habit, but I have. We've painted two-headed Serbian white eagles on the helmets and the army officer, Captain, Major, commands our people. And by co-ordinated action, Kameni, our chief commander in Vukovar, plans the action in co-operation with the army major in the evening, and they carry it out the following day. Because of soldiers deserting from their units, the army did not have enough manpower to go from house to house and take them over, so our people did that. Army strikes with tanks, mortars ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe there was an additional line that would have ended there and so I'll read it from P185, which was that: "Army strikes with tanks, mortars, and howitzers, and our people go from house to house and conquer it." The accused himself said in his "Death of Yugoslavia" interview that during the siege he met with -- the siege of Vukovar, he met with Mrksic and he met with Sljivancanin, and he even claims to have taken part in the combat there, as can be seen in P644, a clip from P644, which we'll play now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I had meetings with General Mrksic, who was the commander of the Guards Brigade which participated in the operations to liberate Vukovar and who commanded our volunteers. Our volunteers were under the direct command of the Chetnik Vojvoda Kameni, Milan Lancuzanin, also known as Kameni, and he was under the command of General Mrksic, commander of the Guards Brigade. I met with him there, spoke to him, inspected the forward lines with him, and so on. He even gave me an army helmet there, onto which I stuck the Chetnik symbol of the double-headed white eagle. This helmet was too small for my head and they later asked me how come the army didn't have any bigger models."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the TO members and volunteers who populated the ranks in Vukovar also had the perception that the accused was linked to them. And this is demonstrated, for example, by Exhibit P25, which is Katic's letter to the SRS War Staff dated 9 December of 1991, in which he signs his signature as the -- excuse me, along with his title as the SRS "Chetnik Commander of Vukovar." And he writes in that letter to the SRS War Staff to "propose warriors for promotion." And as Your Honours would expect, some of the people he proposed were fighters from the LSD, along with -- fighters like Kameni, the commander; Kinez, who it notes was the commander of the LSD's 1st Assault Platoon. But Katic's letter also requests promotion from the SRS Crisis Staff for the members of the TO who the Seseljevci had fought alongside, such as TO members Vujovic, the commander of the local TO; Vujanovic, the chief of the local TO; and Peranovic, commander of the Petrova Gora TO detachment, along with others. Finally, the accused's visits to the front line in Vukovar also ensured that he was well informed and in communication with his men there, his Seseljevci, to whom he was providing constant support and moral -- and encouragement. As the accused himself said during his testimony in the Milosevic trial, which, as the Chamber well knows, is in evidence as Exhibit P31, and this is said at page 542, the accused said: "I went to Vukovar twice while the struggle for liberation was going on. I saw everything. I was at the front lines. I visited almost every street. It is impossible that there was something there that I didn't see." The accused's contribution to the joint criminal enterprise's mission and to the Serb forces in Vukovar was not limited to supplying the manpower. The accused also lent the power of his words, and as Ms. Biersay touched upon in relation to Vukovar, the accused's speeches in and about Vukovar were hateful, they were violent, and the evidence has proven that they had a searing and motiving effect on those who heard them and not just the Seseljevci. His speeches stoked their ethnic hatred and division and they were not just political speeches. The accused was a self-styled military man, and when he appeared in Vukovar he toured that front line wearing a helmet, as you've heard him say, a bullet-proof jacket, and a special JNA camouflage uniform generally worn by high-ranking officers, which was specially made for him. And, Your Honours, I can point you to Exhibit P1058, paragraphs 45 through 46. According to Witness Rankic, as Sljivancanin briefed the accused in Vukovar during his tour of the front line, he called the accused "President" in fronted of all those gathered. And the JNA and police organised his transportation and his security. The effect of all of this, of course, was to boost the accused's influence over the Serb forces he addressed, to lend credibility to his words, and to show that the other authorities in Vukovar -- acting in Vukovar, the other authorities under the control of other JCE members in this case supported the violent and ethnic agenda that the accused espoused. Now, there is no doubt, there is no doubt, that the crimes charged in Vukovar actually occurred. As will be discussed below -- or as I will discuss now, even the accused admits that the crimes happened, and so instead in the brief that he filed he claims that neither he nor his Seseljevci can be linked to them. Now, to begin with, even the accused, while not acknowledging his own responsibility, acknowledged in an interview, which is in evidence as P1225, in fact, re-published by the accused in 1995, that in Vukovar - and these are his words - there was "excessive use of artillery and unrestricted firing of shells without any tactical purpose." That admission is supported by the witness evidence and adjudicated facts which proved that Croatian homes were bombed, that shelling was "indiscriminate" and seemed geared "to wipe out any life from the area." And that's from Exhibit P268 at paragraphs 8, 9, and 15. Targets included the hospital, kindergarten, graveyards, markets, and school buildings. And the shelling continued, as VS-002 described at 6461, even as the Croats put up little resistance. Witness Covic, in P844, page 7, said: "They shelled the entire city irrespective of where the defenders were located." And on 18 November 1991 when Vukovar fell to the Serb forces, the entire city had been razed to the ground. That destruction was not justified by any military purpose, but, Your Honours, there was a two-fold criminal purpose. Because in addition to the physical destruction of Vukovar, the JNA shelling was the means by which large numbers of non-Serbs were forcibly transferred and deported out of the municipality. And, Your Honours, I'll leave this still from P289 as I continue to discuss this topic, but you can see in P289 not only the physical destruction to the town but the lines of people, of residents of that town, forced out of it. Now, the accused is responsible as a JCE member for the effects of the shelling and the bombing, even though he himself was not making the tactical decisions. What happened in Vukovar is a classic example of the JNA tactics observed by the European Monitoring Mission in P412 at page 14 and as described earlier by Mr. Marcussen. The JNA in Vukovar terrorised the population with heavy artillery and then the JNA-backed and armed undisciplined irregulars, Seseljevci amongst them, moved in. So he is responsible because Seseljevci were already active in fields of operation across Croatia as part of the Serb forces, and he is responsible because for at least a significant portion of the time the JNA was bombing Vukovar, Seseljevci were already under the command of Kameni, who was already under the direct command of Mrksic, who was under the control of Kadijevic and Adzic of the JNA. As the accused himself agreed in P644 at pages 12 through 13, the JNA could not have taken Vukovar by "shelling alone." And so war was waged "street by street" by volunteers and the TO, including the Seseljevci. The Seseljevci, along with the other volunteers and TO, contributed to the forced flight in another way as well, by creating an atmosphere of uncertainty, an atmosphere of fear and ethnic hatred which reinforced the need to leave, reinforced the fact that non-Serbs had no choice but to leave if they wanted to survive. For example, according to Witness Emil Cakalic, at transcript page 4954, the song "Slobo, Slobo, there will be plenty of meat, we will slaughter the Croats," "resounded throughout Vukovar" and was sung "especially by volunteers." And I'd ask that P -- the video P58 which demonstrates what he's describing be played now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "There will be plenty of meat. We will slaughter the Croats. "Against the Croats ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And that was the song that can be heard sung by the volunteers you saw marching through P58. The accused's propaganda, as described by Ms. Biersay, labelling every --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, I have to intervene now. The Prosecutor quoted the words from one song, she quoted it, and you can see that from the English transcript. "Slobo, send us salad, there will be meat, we will slaughter the Croats." The interpreter, however, provides completely different verses, i.e., "Croats, we will slaughter you." How come that the interpreter can create the closing argument for the Prosecutor? Please remove that interpreter instantly. These are completely different verses that entail different implications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I didn't get an interpretation of what you just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me in English?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes, now I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like you, please, to ask a replay of --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1110 to 1120, that is where you have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I ask the interpreters to interpret what they hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: May I continue? The interpretation --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I believe that this should entail repercussions. This was not played to the end. But I remind you the Prosecutor very precisely quoted the verses from the song that was sung. At the same time the interpreter, the Croat, provided a totally different interpretation from a song that I have never heard before. To you, this may sound and look similar; however, the implications are very, very different.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, it's Witness Emil Cakalic at transcript page 4954 that gives the quote -- that the song: "Slobo, Slobo, there will be plenty of meat, we will slaughter the Croats" resounded throughout Vukovar and was sung especially by volunteers. The interpretation that I get in English of P58 is exactly that, but in any case, if there are small language differences or language differences from the interpretation, I present to you P58 as an example of this type of song. So may I continue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you will have ten hours to plead, so you will have an opportunity to take up this topic again, and you can challenge the words of the Prosecutor when time comes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Antonetti, I'm not contesting what the Prosecutor is saying. The Prosecutor quoted a somewhat shorter and very true version of the song that was sung by the column. My objection is of an administrative nature. You are duty-bound to issue an order for somebody from the service to listen to the interpretation into the Serbian language, to convince yourself that the interpreter very deliberately provided a very different interpretation. One song is: "Slobo, send us salad, there will be meat, we will slaughter the Croats." However, the song that was provided by the interpreter of his own will states: "Hey, Croats, we will slaughter you, we will slaughter half of you and the rest we will give to the dogs." Do you understand how very, very different the implications of these two songs are? This is not a licencia poética of the interpreter. This is a deliberate deceit. This is not an objection against the Prosecutor's words. This is an administrative objection as a result of the false interpretation, and I have the right to urgently object and you have to undertake measures on my objection. Or maybe you can tell me that I am telling nonsense, you can do that. But this is not something that I should be dealing with in my closing argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Good note has been taken of what you said, and the translation unit will be asked to verify and to write a report about this interpretation issue. Mrs. Prosecutor, you can go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I apologise. In addition to the discriminatory and persecutory songs that rang throughout Vukovar, as we've just heard and seen, the accused's propaganda, labelling every Croat as an Ustasha, infected the mind-set of the Serb forces in Vukovar and to them the evidence has shown every Croat was an Ustasha, and volunteers openly killed unarmed Croats. For example, Witness Stojanovic, in P528, paragraphs 40 to 41, stated that Kameni issued an order to kill any Croats and further that "volunteers engaged in cleansing the area told us that when they found Croats, they killed them on the spot, armed or not, because they did not have time to take them to Velepromet, where there was a collection centre and a prison. Kameni himself ordered our group, which guarded houses, to execute any Croats we found on the spot." Witness Stojanovic went on to describe seeing Seseljevci "from Kameni's group" beat and then slit the throats of five unarmed Croats in front of about 30 people. According to Witness Stojanovic, the JNA called in Kameni and Kinez, his deputy, as a result but they were not arrested and they remained in command of the LSD. And that, Your Honours, is at P526, paragraphs 26 and 27. Stojanovic, Witness Stojanovic, confirmed this information in both P526, which was -- which he gave in August 2004, and again in P528, his statement from June 2006. And for further discussion of the credibility of those -- and reliability of those written statements, I refer the Chamber back to our discussion in the brief and the argumentative appendix. VS-034 also confirmed the Seseljevci's brutal treatment of detainees and gave evidence that he was ordered by Kameni to murder detainees. And, Your Honour, for that I refer the Court to Exhibits P1058 at paragraphs 39, 42 to -- 42 and 43, and P1056, paragraph 31. The violence and persecutions in Vukovar committed by the Serb forces, and specifically by the volunteers and Seseljevci, was open, it was accepted, and it was exacted without fear of repercussion from the accused or from any other political and military leader who controlled or contributed to those Serb forces and who are the named JCE members in this case. And of the few non-Serbs who remained by the end of the siege of Vukovar, many were later forcibly transferred out by the bus-load, some to Croatian areas of what remained of Croatia; and others across borders to Serbia and then on from there. And although the accused later publicly questioned the JNA shelling tactics, Your Honours, he may not rely on that now to escape criminal responsibility because the evidence has proven that he supported the implementation of the JCE's common purpose, the JCE's common plan by any means possible, including the occurrence of crimes such as the wanton destruction of the town. And thus, in Exhibit P1225 at page 6, in the same interview where he criticises the JNA tactics of overusing artillery, he added that he would "always celebrate the liberation of Vukovar." I now turn specifically to the murders, torture, and cruel treatment and persecutions at Ovcara, Grabovo, and Velepromet on the 19th to 21st of November, 1991. Again, these crimes are so well established that they are simply undeniable. As the accused said during the testimony of Vilim Karlovic, and I quote the accused: "I am not challenging the crime. I have never challenged it. A terrible crime did take place and there's no doubt about that." So again, unable to challenge the crime, the accused denies any link to the physical perpetrators in his final submission. But the accused is responsible for those crimes because the Serb forces were still in control and operating during the time-period when the crimes at Velepromet, Ovcara, and Grabovo occurred. He is responsible because his Seseljevci were amongst the physical perpetrators and are both linked to him and to other JCE members through the TO and the JNA, and he is responsible because the other physical perpetrators themselves, JNA, TO, and other volunteers, are linked to his fellow JCE members. The continued co-operation of these Serb forces on the 19th to the 21st November is demonstrated by the evidence in numerous ways. For example, members of the JNA knew that the TO and volunteers were exacting violence upon the non-Serb prisoners of war throughout the siege of Vukovar. And there are extreme examples of this throughout the record. For example, when JNA Major Lukic was told about Seseljevci looting and cutting off the ears of a prisoner, and he chose not to punish them because volunteers were needed on the front lines. And for that, Your Honours, I can refer you to Exhibit P857, at paragraphs 57 to 58. Or Sljivancanin's 19 November warning about Velepromet that "Chetniks are slaughtering there." Despite the knowledge of what was happening, Sljivancanin deliberately prevented access to the hospital by the Red Cross until the detainees had been taken from the hospital and were on their way to the JNA barracks. And it was the JNA that re-routed the detainees to the Ovcara hangar from the barracks after a meeting at which including JNA, TO, and members of the SAO SBWS government, including JCE members such as Arkan and Hadzic, were present. Some members of the JNA were then at the barracks, participating in the beatings itself, while others took no action to stop it. Miodrag Panic, the highest-ranking JNA officer on the scene, left. The JNA military police who were supposed to be there to protect the detainees withdrew at Mrksic's order. The testimony of Josip Covic also illustrates the co-ordination and the clear chain of authority that was still in effect at Velepromet on 20 November 1991. He told of how the JNA and TO together drove people, including civilians, the elderly and infirm, and hors de combat fighters, away from the hospital, the Vukovar hospital. He told how the men were then separated by TO members and then it was a JNA officer who ordered them taken to Velepromet. Once at Velepromet, a group of detainees were separated out and civilians allowed to point to some amongst them, after which the TO called Seseljevci to take those selected people behind the hangar and to kill them. One Seseljevac slit a man's throat in front of the rest of the detainees. As Covic himself was beaten by people he described as Chetniks, a JNA officer called the men beating him away, not to stop them from beating him, which he testified nobody there tried to do, but to go fulfil another one of their orders. A JNA major then ordered Covic and the other detainees onto buses to Sremska Mitrovica. Victims Emil Cakalic, Vilim Karlovic, and Dragutin Berghofer similarly told what occurred at Ovcara and they are corroborated by others, by victims, perpetrators, and observers alike, including Vesna Bosanac, JNA officers Vukasinovic and Vojnovic, and protected witnesses VS-051, 16, 21, 65, 2, and others. The testimony of these witnesses which proved so unassailably that the crimes occurred also prove the accused's guilt for the murders and abuses at Ovcara and Grabovo beyond a reasonable doubt. The evidence proved that when JNA Witness Vukasinovic arrived at the hospital on the 20th of November with the buses that had been ordered by Major Sljivancanin, the commanders of the TO detachments, including Miroljub Vujovic, Stanko Vujanovic, and Kameni, were there with their fighters along with Sljivancanin. Men of all ages, including the wounded, the elderly, and minors, were taken and herded onto buses. They were brought to the JNA barracks and eventually to the hangar at Ovcara. Kameni, along with others, escorted the first group of buses. With the JNA present, detainees were forced to run through a gauntlet of TO and volunteers, who some described as Chetniks, who beat them and taunted them, and as VS-016 recounted at transcript 11129, taunted them with ethnic slurs such as: "Beat the Ustasha cunts." Inside that hangar, members of the JNA, TO, and volunteers including people who were identified as Seseljevci, beat the detainees. VS-065 reported that Stanko Vujanovic, Miroljub Vujovic and Seseljevac Kameni were the TO commanders on the scene. Some of the beaters wore the Chetnik insignia and had the four Cs on their caps or wore fur hats. Someone blew a whistle to indicate when beatings should stop and start. And they sang persecutory songs like "Bring out the salad and we'll have meat because we're going to slaughter the Croats." And that was from the testimony of Mr. Karlovic at transcript 4779, the quote. One survivor recalled watching a man beaten to death while he was forced to sing Chetnik songs and to lick the boots of his attacker. Beatings lasted for several hours, and sometime after 2100 hours, TO commander Miroljub Vujovic ordered the first group of detainees out of the hangar and into a trailer bound for Grabovo and the pit that had already been dug. Several trips were made bringing additional prisoners of war to their deaths. Witnesses VS-016, VS-065, and Stoparic, at transcript 2357 and 2360, identified people who were members of the LSD as being among the volunteers -- I'm sorry, as being among the volunteers, TO, and JNA members who brought the detainees to the pit. And the same combination of forces also made up the firing squads who shot and in some cases stabbed the detainees to death. According to VS-002, when they ran short on ammunition at the pit, Vujovic, the TO commander, went to the JNA to get more. And that can be found at transcript 6549. The evidence thus proves beyond a reasonable doubt that Kameni and the LSD, along with the other TO commanders and their fighters, were part of the organised removal of people from the hospital overseen by the JNA, and that they followed the prisoners from there under the protection of the JNA, which was still clearly in a position of authority, they followed them to Ovcara and ultimately all the way to their death at the Grabovo pit. And those events clearly demonstrate that the accused is linked to the physical perpetrators of those crimes. Your Honour, the lengths that the accused goes to in his brief to distance himself from those physical perpetrators betrays a willingness to assert as facts information that is wholly unsupported in the record and without basis in truth. His efforts to deny his link to those crimes are remarkable in his submission -- to deny his links to those crimes in his submission are remarkable for their lack of credibility. First, the accused claims that there were no more SRS volunteers in Vukovar when the crimes at Ovcara, Grabovo, and Velepromet were committed. Now, aside from the extensive witness evidence already discussed, which places the LSD and its Seseljevci still in Vukovar, still taking orders from the TO and working with the JNA at the time when the murders and abuse occurred, there is definitive documentary evidence that the accused's assertion is not true and that is at Exhibit P41. Mrksic's order regulating the issue of resubordination and the return of the home units. This order clearly shows that on the 20th of November, when the Serb forces, including Seseljevci, were committing those crimes, the LSD was still in Vukovar and still subordinated to the JNA. Next, the accused asserts in his brief that no SRS volunteer has been linked to any crime, and to back up this assertion in his brief, the accused incredibly disavows his connection to his Vojvoda Kameni and the fighters under his command, now drawing a distinction between Seseljevci sent to Vukovar from elsewhere and those from Vukovar and its environs. He even relies in his brief on the assertion that Kameni was just a reserve JNA member from Vukovar and not a member of the SRS. Your Honours, would this be a good time to take the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have been sitting for approximately an hour and a half. We shall have a break and resume around ten minutes to 11.00. We shall have a break at 12.25 and have a break because a new Judge is being appointed today. That should last 20 minutes or so. And after that, we will resume after the swearing-in ceremony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, when we broke I was turning to the accused's next argument in his brief in which he disavowed his relationship to Kameni and the Seseljevci under his command and relied on the assertion that Kameni was just a reserve JNA member from Vukovar and not a member of the SRS. And while Kameni was from Vukovar and was a reserve JNA officer, it is indisputable that he was a Seseljevac, whether or not he was a member of the SRS, which in fact anyway he was. He commanded Seseljevci, he reported to the accused, and there is an unbreakable link between Kameni and the LSD and the accused. And for that I would draw the Chamber's attention, in addition to the videos that we already saw where the accused mentions Kameni and the other testimony discussed, to Exhibits P255, page 3; P185, page 1; transcript 3429 to 3435; Exhibit P288, page 1; transcript 5075 to 5077; and Exhibit P217, page 3; and in fact to the accused's own testimony in Milosevic about Kameni's SRS membership. Of course, Exhibit P31 at page 627. Seselj's order, the accused's order, appointing Kameni Vojvoda commends him -- commends Kameni as having been with "the Serbian Chetnik Movement since its establishment." And describes him as the "commander of Leva Supoderica Volunteers Unit of the Serbian Radical Party and Serbian Chetnik Movement." And that is at Exhibit P217, page 3. The accused's connection not just to Kameni but to every fighter under Kameni's command in the LSD was so well established that, as Ms. Biersay mentioned earlier, even the JNA referred to the fighters in that detachment by the name Seseljevci in official communications. And I would point to Exhibit P41, page 2. Now, the accused in his brief next makes a legal argument that the judgement in the case of Mrksic, Sljivancanin, and Radic, that in that case there was not sufficient evidence to find a JCE had been proven beyond a reasonable doubt, the accused argues that that precludes this Chamber from finding him responsible for the crimes in Vukovar under a JCE or, in fact, under any other theory. The Mrksic Trial Chamber found no joint criminal enterprise had been proven between those three accused in relation to the limited common purpose alleged in that indictment which was "the persecution of Croats or other non-Serbs who were present in the Vukovar Hospital after the fall of Vukovar." And that's from the Mrksic indictment, Your Honours, at paragraphs 5 through 7. The JCE, the joint criminal enterprise, charged in this case is defined by a different common purpose, that of the permanent forcible removal, through the commission of the enumerated crimes, of a majority of the non-Serb population from approximately one-third of the territory of Croatia and large parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to make it part of a new Serb-dominated state. And, Your Honours, that's of course in this indictment, paragraph 6. So the existence of the JCE in this indictment aimed at a significantly larger geographic area, a more broadly defined population with a differently defined common purpose is not affected by that judgement. Next, the Mrksic appeals judgement does not preclude this Chamber from finding the accused guilty of persecution as a crime against humanity for the killings at Ovcara and Grabovo, as the accused argues in his brief that it does. His argument -- his argument is that the Appeals Chamber's finding in Mrksic that the killings did not have a nexus with the widespread and systematic attack on the civilian population constitutes an effective estoppel for this Chamber, and that is not correct. First, the subjective knowledge of the physical perpetrators is not crucial to determining the liability of the accused pursuant to the JCE. The Mrksic Appeals Chamber had to determine there whether the physical perpetrators' subjective knowledge fulfilled the nexus requirements of crimes against humanity because at that point the Chamber was focusing on whether the accused were guilty of aiding and abetting rather than committing those crimes. However, when the mode under consideration is JCE, it is the JCE members' subjective knowledge which is relevant, irrespective of whether the physical perpetrator has that knowledge. And for further discussion of this point, I would point the Chamber to the Milutinovic judgement at paragraphs 158 to 162. The accused and his fellow JCE members in this case, including the JNA commanders Adzic and Kadijevic, and also including Arkan and Goran Hadzic, both of whom, the latter two, played critical roles in the hand-over of the prisoners of war to the TO and volunteers directly as well as the JNA members, they all had knowledge that there was an attack on the civilian population and that the attacks committed by the physical perpetrators were part of that attack. The evidence of the knowledge of the JCE members in this case is set out at length in the Prosecution's final trial submission, final trial brief, at, amongst others, paragraphs 136 to 146, 181 to 182, and 194 to 195. Second, this case is distinguishable from the Mrksic case on its facts. The widespread and systematic attack on the civilian population in this case has a greater geographic and temporal scope, and therefore purpose, to the attack considered in Mrksic. The attack in this case was against the non-Serb population, as I've said, in one-third of the territory of Croatia and a significant portion of Bosnia and Herzegovina, compared with an attack limited to the civilian population of Vukovar in that case. A much broader range of factors are thus relevant to determining whether the underlying crimes at Ovcara and Grabovo have a nexus to this widespread and systematic attack against the civilian population, as defined in this case. And the evidence in this case demonstrates that the JCE members aimed to rid a large geographic area of all non-Serbs, whether civilian or otherwise. The Ovcara and Grabovo victims' status must be considered in the context of acts committed against those non-Serbs as a whole. This Chamber consequently heard significantly different evidence than the Mrksic Chamber regarding the removal of and crimes committed against the targeted non-Serb population of Croatia and of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, as I previously noted in relation to Vukovar during the siege and as is discussed in the Prosecution's final trial brief at paragraphs 108 to 125, in relation to the larger Croatian campaign, other murders, abuse, and persecutions against both hors de combat non-Serb fighters and civilians had already been perpetrated as part of the larger campaign of persecutions throughout the region and they would go on to be perpetrated throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. The primary consideration for all of these victims was that they were non-Serb. That the physical perpetrators at Ovcara and Grabovo singled out for harsher treatment those who they perceived as being hors de combat doesn't sever the required connection in this case on this evidence to this attack as it has been defined. Thus, whether the Chamber is looking at these killings through the lens of the JCE or whether the Chamber is considering the other modes of liability, like aiding and abetting or instigation, the Mrksic Chamber's findings are not binding because that Chamber examined whether the acts of the physical perpetrators had a nexus with a completely different attack, one that was of a much smaller scope and a much smaller purpose. If the Chamber should nonetheless find that no crimes against humanity have been proven under Article 5, the accused is still responsible for the murders, torture, and cruel treatment at Ovcara and Grabovo under Article 3. The accused is also charged with the direct commission of persecution for his speeches regarding Vukovar, one made in Vukovar and one made in Sid, and I will address his claims regarding these charges briefly now. First, the accused is charged in regard to the speech he made in Sid on 7 November 1991, in which he stated that the Serb TO of the SAO SBWS was at work in the region and that as a result "this entire area will soon be cleared of Ustasha." His words were reported in the "Politika" article that's in evidence as P1285, as he intended that they would be reported since he made the statement at a press conference. At the time, Sid had temporary barracks set up to arm volunteers. It was close to the front in Vukovar, and the accused made the statement as part of his press tour en route to Vukovar to encourage the troops there just at the time when Serb forces were gearing up for a final push and tensions were running especially high. Regarding the accused's infamous statement that "no Ustasha shall leave Vukovar alive," the accused now adamantly denies ever making the statement and relies heavily on the Mrksic Chamber's discussion of VS-027. But in his brief, the accused misrepresents that Chamber's opinion of that witness's evidence. At paragraph 364, the Mrksic Trial Chamber expressed certain concerns about aspects of the testimony, but noted that they accepted parts of the testimony, where it was corroborated by credible, independent evidence. And in this case, Your Honours, that testimony, the testimony that the accused said while in Vukovar before its fall, that "no Ustasha shall leave Vukovar alive," is corroborated by credible, independent evidence, evidence which was not heard in the Mrksic case. The statements of Zoran Rankic, a close associate of the accused, who gave evidence, in Exhibit P1074 at paragraph 69, that he was with the accused throughout his trip to Vukovar and recalls the accused pronouncing "not one Ustasha is to leave Vukovar alive." He recalls him making this statement to at least 50 people, including volunteers, TO members, and officers of the Guards Brigade, including Sljivancanin and Radic. And people fired in the air in support of his words. Rankic's statement in P1074 in this regard is unambiguous and it should be relied upon, and he acknowledged the accuracy of that statement -- of P1074 in multiple subsequent statements. And for further discussion again of Rankic's credibility, I would refer the Trial Chamber to the final trial brief, paragraphs 3 through 7, and the argumentative appendix. There is further corroboration from VS-016, who also heard the accused repeat those words as he stood on Nova Ulica, next to the LSD headquarters. The accused declared that "not a single Ustasha should leave Vukovar alive" to the gathered group, which included Seseljevci, including Kameni and others, policemen, JNA soldiers, TO members, and other fighters. And in response to the accused's statement, the fighters all raised their rifles as a sign of approval. And that, Your Honour, is from VS-016's recounting. At transcript 11121, 11171 to 72, 11288. Witnesses' differing recollections of the exact circumstances under which the statement was made by the accused suggests that the accused, as he is wont to do, repeated those words in some variation throughout his visit. And additionally as discussed in the brief, the Prosecution's final trial brief at paragraph 155, the crimes at Ovcara, Grabovo, and throughout Vukovar can be directly attributed to those who heard his remarks or those under the command and influence of other people who heard them. The accused's strenuous denials that he ever uttered these words are all the more unreliable since in his 84 bis statement in front of this Chamber - at transcript 1921 to 1922, while denying that he made the infamous statement specifically to troops in Vukovar - the accused was forced to acknowledge that it was possible that "at somewhere, sometime, I said something like that." And it was telling when testifying in the Milosevic trial at -- in P31 at page 581, he used the very same phrase: "It was always my standpoint that the Ustasha had to be defeated and that not a single Ustasha could leave alive, but that they should all be caught." Witness Stojanovic, himself a Seseljevac, who was motivated to join the war effort by one of the accused's speeches, as he explained in P528 at paragraph 8, reported that the accused's audience understood his message when he spoke. As Stojanovic said at -- in P528 at paragraph 12, he understood that: "One of Seselj's objectives was to cleanse parts of Croatia that he considered to be Serbian land." And referring to the other fighters that heard the words -- that heard Seselj's words with him, Stojanovic said: "Other people understood it the same way." The accused understood and intended the persecutory nature of his statements. And as he himself conceded in an interview in Exhibit P50, page 8 [sic], his statements against non-Serbs and calling for the expulsion of non-Serbs could have caused those who listened to him to hate non-Serbs. And nor were these his only such statements. Seselj made other similar statements in Vukovar, the accused did, in Vukovar which provoked equally strong reactions. VS-034 recalled, in P1058 at paragraph 46, watching the accused address the soldiers in Vukovar, and saying that: "Ustasha should be expelled." And recounted how the volunteers responded, and what he said was that the volunteers responded by singing: "Croats, we shall slaughter you, slaughter you a bit but give you to the dogs more often." And, Your Honours, that concludes the portion of the presentation on -- regarding the charged crimes in Vukovar municipality, and I would like to now hand the floor over to Mr. Mussemeyer, who will be addressing the pattern municipalities of Vocin, Bijeljina, Bosanski Samac, and Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the JCE members and their forces implemented their common purpose similarly throughout the regions they targeted, as Mr. Marcussen has explained. Four key patterns were repeated throughout the conflict, these were: First, arming and military training of Serb local population; second, volunteers and paramilitaries, including Seseljevci, arrived in the area; third, Serbs took over the municipalities and created separate Serb authorities; and fourth, Serb forces, including Seseljevci, committed crimes, including killing of non-Serbs, forcible transfer, detention and mistreatment in facilities controlled by local authorities, and destruction of cultural monuments. The repeated occurrence of the same patterns demonstrates that a common plan developed and executed by the JCE members was behind the take-over of these municipalities. The patterns of implementation of the JCE happened first in Croatia. Evidence of those patterns, and the accused's involvement in implementing them, goes back to the arming of Serb forces in Borovo Selo and the arrival of Seseljevci there. My colleague Ms. Hochhauser described the crimes that were later committed nearby, in Vukovar, and similar events were repeated in the Bosnian crime-base locations. These patterns carried through from the Serb campaign in Croatia to the crimes in Vukovar and then to the first pattern municipality in this case, which is Vocin. The pattern of events was similar and some of the perpetrators were even redeployed from Vukovar to Western Slavonia. After the crimes in Vocin, as Mr. Marcussen discussed, the JCE members shifted their focus from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina. The same patterns carried through there. They were seen in the municipalities of Bijeljina, Bosanski Samac, and Brcko, and then the same forces and some of the same fighters would implement the common purpose in the Bosnian crime-base municipalities. The accused and his Seseljevac were involved in the implementation of the common purpose in all four municipalities. I will now summarise the events in Vocin. Witness Maretic testified that local Serbs in Western Slavonia started arming themselves after the elections in Croatia in 1990. By August 1991, paramilitary formations and a local Serb TO were present in the area. That month, Serb forces took over Vocin. Witness Matovina testified that local TO leader Boro Lukic occupied the police station in Vocin, took down and burned the Croatian flag, and hoisted the Serbian flag in its place. Shortly afterwards, armed Serb forces occupied Vocin. Shooting from machine-guns and automatic weapons could be heard. When the shooting stopped, Lukic told Croats to surrender their weapons. Serb forces searched Croats' houses for weapons. Soon thereafter, Serbs established separate Serb authorities in the SAO Western Slavonia. On 27 September 1991, the commander of the TO municipal staff of Podravska Slatina ordered that regional departments of Vocin police station be formed. The new departments were staffed by Serb officers who served in the Croatian police before. Most Serb police officers did not return their weapons when they left the Croatian police. In October 1991, paramilitaries, including Seseljevci and White Eagles, arrived in Vocin by civilian buses. The commander of Seselj's men was Radovan Novacic. Other Seseljevci, after taking part in conquering and destroying Vukovar, were deployed [sic] to Western Slavonia. The JNA armed these Seseljevci and paid their salaries. The volunteers had a very bad reputation among the local population. They walked around with weapons, came into courtyards asking for alcohol. They scared the local inhabitants. The accused visited his volunteers in Vocin in late November 1991. In Sekulinci Lager he gave a speech to his volunteers, and yet, after his visit, tensions rose and the Seseljevci actually became more violent and started killing civilian Croats. Crimes had occurred throughout the Serb campaign in Western Slavonia. 22 civilians were killed during the Serb forces' attack on Cetekovac, Cojlug, and Balinci. Volunteers abducted non-Serbs and brought them to Sekulinci Lager where they were maltreated and even killed some detainees. At the beginning of December volunteers torched Croats' houses. Around the 4th December, four young Croat men who had to perform forced labour for Serb forces were killed by Seseljevci. By 8 December 1991, ethnic Croats had entirely vacated the nearby municipalities of Grubisno Polje and Daruvar due to the conflict. In the night from the 12th to the 13th of December, 1991, 45 elderly non-Serbs were murdered. We viewed Exhibit P435, showing victims whose bodies were mutilated and some were burned. Witness Matovina, the police officer supervising the criminal investigations after the killing, discovered during his investigations that Seseljevci were among the perpetrators. Witness Kulic corroborated this. Serb forces blew up the Catholic church in Vocin. We have seen Exhibit P437, a video-clip showing the ruins of the church. Houses at Vocin were torched and looted. The day after the explosion Witness Matovina came to Vocin and he testified that it "looked like Hiroshima." After the crimes in Vocin, many Croat inhabitants fled the village. A list of refugees who fled Vocin is in evidence as Exhibit P434. In his closing brief, the accused denies that there was a pattern and that the JCE existed in relation to Vocin. But he did not contest that the events happened in Vocin, which I just summarised. His Seseljevci were in Vocin, he visited his volunteers there. The accused did not contest the killing of 49 non-Serbs in Vocin, but he disputes that his men were involved in the crimes. However, Matovina, Maretic, Kulic, VS-018, and VS-033 all provide evidence which demonstrate that the Seseljevci perpetrated crimes in Vocin, just as they had in Vukovar and throughout the JCE campaign in Croatia. I will now turn to the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992, which show the same characteristic pattern I described in the beginning, namely, arming and military training of local Serb population; arrival of volunteers and paramilitaries, including Seseljevci; Serbs taking control over the municipalities and creation of separate Serb authorities; the commission of crimes. This pattern repeated in the Bosnian municipalities relevant to this indictment, the first of those municipalities was Bijeljina. The take-over of Bijeljina was led by the accused's Vojvoda Mirko Blagojevic. Here on Exhibit P737, you can see his role during the take-over.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Shoot at the ... "Mirko Blagojevic: I am the president of the Serbian Radical Party Regional Board. We actually control all the accesses to the city and all exits from it too, and we control approximately 75 per cent of the city."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: The accused and Blagojevic discussed the take-over and ethnic cleansing of Bijeljina before the war. Witness VS-1028 overheard a conversation in the Café Srbija where they discussed how to cleanse Bijeljina of non-Serbs. They agreed to kill non-Serbs and agreed that anybody who remained and was not loyal would be expelled to Turkey or Croatia. Vojvoda Blagojevic, together with Arkan's men, then organised arming and training of the local population. Arkan's men were deployed in the surrounding areas of Bijeljina before the conflict began. The accused admitted that JCE member Biljana Plavsic brought Arkan and his men to Bijeljina. Along with the deployment of paramilitaries, JCE members began creating separate Serb institutions in Bijeljina. Republika Srpska Minister of Interior Momcilo Mandic instructed police commanders, among them the chief of police from Bijeljina, to prepare for separation, including arming of Serb police officers and the police station. And I refer to adjudicated fact number 179. Witness VS-1035, a Muslim police officer, had to sign a declaration to be loyal to the Serbian SUP. The take-over of Bijeljina started on the night of the 31st of March, 1992. VS-1028 realised that his Serb neighbours left their homes before the attack. Blagojevic commanded the Seseljevci who participated in the take-over. He and his men co-operated with Arkan's men and JNA units. The accused boasted on several occasions that Bijeljina was liberated by Vojvoda Blagojevic and his men, for instance, in Exhibits P682; P685, page 11; and P1242, page 10. During the take-over, many non-Serb civilians were killed. A member of Blagojevic's unit known as Suma killed a father and two sons. Arkan's men killed members of the Sabanovic family and one of Arkan's men can be seen in this slide abusing their bodies. And when the fighting was over, Witness 1035 was ordered to provide protection to the people who collected the corpses in the streets and cellars in Bijeljina. He testified that they collected 48 bodies. Many non-Serb inhabitants were arrested and mistreated by the MUP. In Batkovic camp, close to Bijeljina, prisoners were regularly beaten and subjected to forced labour. Some were killed. The horrible conditions in the detention camps in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including Bijeljina, were noted by this Chamber in its first adjudicated facts decision number 293 and 297. And Serb forces destroyed non-Serb religious and cultural monuments. Expert Riedlmayer's report shows that monuments throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina were systematically destroyed. In Bijeljina, all 15 non-Serb religious and cultural monuments were damaged, and 12 of the Muslim religious buildings were either completely destroyed or almost destroyed. Riedlmayer often found a huge garbage container where the mosque has one been. I will now show five characteristic examples of the destruction of cultural monuments in Bosnia. The examples are all taken from Exhibit 1045, the annex to Riedlmayer's report. And I will show pictures -- two pictures from before and after the destruction. First picture. This first example is the destructed Krpic mosque in Bijeljina. The picture on the left shows the mosque before the destruction and the picture on the right how the place of the mosque looked after the destruction. On the second after-destruction photo, you also see a garbage container Riedlmayer talked about during his testimony. The second example is the Azizija mosque in Brcko. You see --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
