utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, this is a show for the public, first and foremost. Therefore, I would kindly ask Mr. Mussemeyer to say about every mosque when it was actually destroyed. It is very important for this to be known. I'm sure that he has the data about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's absolutely not normal for you to interrupt the Prosecutor during his presentation, and I would tell you the same if you had the floor. The accused is supposed to speak last and he speaks last in order to be given the opportunity to challenge what has been said before, and in particular things like the Prosecutor has shown pictures of this kind and that kind, et cetera. And this has already been said when the expert witness testified about these mosques. You made the same remark then. So the Chamber knows perfectly well that there may be a problem in the dates. Mr. Prosecutor, you can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: The second example is the Azizija mosque in Brcko. You see how the mosque looked before the conflict and what remained. You see in the picture on the right an empty place. The third example shows the before and after picture of the Azizija mosque in Bosanski Samac. Again, you see a huge garbage container on the empty place where once the mosque was standing. The next two examples refer to destroyed Catholic churches, and again you see the situation before and after destruction. The first picture shows the Roman Catholic Parish Church of the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus in Bosanski Samac. What is interesting on the after-destruction picture is the undamaged Orthodox church opposite to the empty place where the Catholic church used to stay. The last example is the Roman Catholic Parish Church of St. Anthony the Hermit in Gorice, in Brcko. In his closing brief the accused contested that his men co-operated with Arkan's men during the take-over of Bijeljina. However, Witnesses VS-1028 and Gusalic described the Seseljevci's co-operation with Arkan's men in Bijeljina. The accused challenges the credibility of VS-1028, asserting that the witness expected to be provided with means to live abroad if he testified against the accused, but the accused ignores that the witness testified that he got his residency permit in the country where he lives today without the help of this Tribunal and before he testified in this case. Further, the accused is correct that local Seseljevci led by Mirko Blagojevic participated in the take-over of Bijeljina where they committed crimes. It is irrelevant that these Seseljevci were not from Serbia. The accused was directly involved in the take-over. He met with Blagojevic to discuss ethnically cleansing Bijeljina and bragged that Blagojevic liberated the municipality, as I already mentioned. And after the take-over and crimes in Bijeljina, Blagojevic still shares the accused's ideas of Greater Serbia and celebrated the JCE members' persecutory campaign. I will now turn to the events in Bosanski Samac. The pattern that Vojvoda Blagojevic helped implement in Bijeljina were soon repeated in Bosanski Samac. The JNA armed local Serbs in the Bosanski Samac region to advance the common purpose of the JCE. In addition, the local MUP leadership sent 20 Serbs to a MUP training camp for special training. On 29th February, 1992, local Serbs created a Serb municipality of Bosanski Samac, which is Exhibit P670. This led to conflict because non-Serbs in the area did not accept the Serbian proclamation that the entire territory was theirs. Shortly after the first take-over in North-Eastern Bosnia, the first Seseljevci arrived in Bosanski Samac by JNA helicopter from a Red Berets training camp in Serbia. The night before, the head of the Red Berets, JCE member Frenki Simatovic, had visited the camp to instruct the Seseljevci on their upcoming task in Bosnia. Days later, in Bijeljina, ethnic Serbs temporarily evacuated Bosanski Samac and then Serb forces took over the municipality. As local Serb leader Blagoje Simic informed the JNA, a Crisis Staff was established and paramilitaries and police took control of the most important facilities in the town. Their goal was to ethnically cleanse Bosanski Samac. Seseljevci Srecko Radovanovic, aka Debeli, and Slobodan Miljkovic, aka Lugar, were among the paramilitaries who participated in the take-over as the accused admitted in the Milosevic case. The accused appointed Debeli Vojvoda in May 1993. He contests that Lugar was an SRS member when he was in Bosanski Samac. But Exhibit P1041 shows that already in 1991 Lugar had asked the accused to become a Seseljevac and went to Slavonia as a member of the SRS. The consequences of the take-over for non-Serbs from Bosanski Samac was drastic. A good example which demonstrates the atmosphere and the discriminatory measures taken against non-Serbs after the take-over is an order signed by Stevan Todorovic of the local public police station which is in evidence in P673, and I will quote it. It says, first: "It is forbidden for three or more Muslims or Croats to gather together in public places." Second: "Any such group should be first warned, and if the offence is repeated, the participants should be apprehended and arrested." Third: "For the fulfilment of this order, the commander of the military police platoon and the commander of the public safety stations are personally responsible." Because of this order, Muslims could not even have funeral processions, as Witness Sulejman Tihic testified. Along with these discriminatory measures, other indictment crimes were commonplace in Bosanski Samac. This Chamber has judicially noticed that Serb forces set up detention facilities in Bosanski Samac which were full of people who had no weapons and nothing to do with arming or armed groups. More than 1.500 non-Serbs were detained at sites including the TO building and the secondary schools in Bosanski Samac and the Omladinski Dom in Crkvina. The detainees were abused and some were murdered. Witness Tihic and VS-1000 testified that one of the worst perpetrators was Seseljevac Slobodan Miljkovic, aka Lugar. Lugar participated in a massacre in Crkvina where 16 non-Serb prisoners were murdered and killed the prison inmate nicknamed Dikan. As occurred throughout Bosnia, non-Serb religious sites were also destroyed in Bosanski Samac. Here I refer, for instance, as we have just seen, to the Catholic Parish Church of the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus which was completely destroyed. The Orthodox church across the street, however, was undamaged, suggesting that the Catholic church was intentionally targeted. In his closing brief, the accused alleges that Seseljevci are not linked to the perpetrators of the crimes in Bosanski Samac. However, this link is clearly demonstrated by Witnesses VS-1058, VS-1000, VS-1010, and Sulejman Tihic. I will finally turn to the events in Brcko. Seseljevci under Blagojevic arrived from Bijeljina to Brcko. Also, Arkan's men participated in the take-over of Brcko. Before the paramilitaries arrived, Witness 1033 observed JNA helicopters landing at the barracks and soldiers wearing red berets leaving the helicopter. Later he saw Red Berets training local Serbs in self-defence. The JNA distributed weapons to local Serbs, street signs appeared indicating Brcko was now part of a separate Serb region, SAO Semberija and Majevica or SAO Serbian Krajina. On 30th April 1992, Serb forces started to take over Brcko by blowing up the two bridges over the Sava River. The actual fighting began during the night of the 2nd May 1992. Arkan's men and Seseljevci under Blagojevic participated in the take-over, as they already had in Bijeljina. A JNA aircraft bombed the town, while the attack on Brcko was carried out by groups of mixed members of Serb forces, military police of the JNA, Serb volunteers, Red Berets, and Seseljevci. This has all been testified by Witness VS-1033. The crimes which characterised the JCE campaign also occurred in Brcko. The day when the take-over began, policemen and soldiers massacred a group of civilians outside the local market. Witness VS-1033 observed similar situations to the photos showing Goran Jelisic killing a civilian. Many people died in the area and Witness 1033 personally witnessed soldiers dumping bodies from a refrigerator truck into a mass grave. Non-Serbs were detained at Luka camp in the Brcko harbour area. Blagojevic and his Seseljevci arrived at the camp. Blagojevic gave speeches and his men tortured the inmates in his presence. One Seseljevac carved a cross into the forehead of a Muslim inmate with a knife. And one member of Serb forces, Goran Jelisic, tortured inmates and bragged that he had already killed 97 non-Serbs. Expert Riedlmayer --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, again there is a huge problem with the interpreter. Here Mr. Mussemeyer said Blagojevic and Seseljevci arrived in the Luka camp, and the interpreter says Blagojevic and Seselj arrived at the camp. Are you going to tolerate, to keep on tolerating that interpreter? Please listen to the recording in the Serbian and look at the transcript to check what Mr. Mussemeyer actually said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, what you hear in your language -- we don't know what you hear because what we see is the screen with the transcript in English and we hear the French interpretation. So what you hear is not of our knowledge. Therefore, if, as you just said, the Prosecutor has said that Blagojevic and the Seseljevci arrived, whereas you heard that Blagojevic came together with you, yes, indeed, there's a difference between these two sentences. But what did the Prosecutor say, that the -- that Blagojevic came with the Seseljevci or that he came with Seselj?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I did say with Seseljevci. He did not come with Seselj himself, but he come with Seseljevci, Seselj's men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. In that case I will ask the interpreters to clearly distinguish between the men of Seselj, the Seselj's men, and Seselj in person. You can go on, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you are now mocking my objection. You're making fun of it. We are not talking about whether the interpreter is going to make a distinction between myself and Seselj's men. It's a more important issue as to whether the interpreter is going to interpret properly or not. You are taking every opportunity to mock me, but you're actually mocking the Hague Tribunal, not me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, no one turning you -- is making fun of you. You made a remark and the Chamber has noted your remark, and I have invited the interpreters to be quite careful. Mr. Prosecutor, you can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I will now discuss the destruction of cultural monuments in Brcko. Expert Riedlmayer has listed 21 damaged cultural monuments, 12 Muslim and 9 Catholic religious buildings in Brcko. Seven mosques were completely and one almost destroyed. Three were heavily and only one was lightly damaged. From the damaged Catholic churches, seven were heavily and two lightly damaged. In his brief, the accused alleges that the crimes in Brcko were not linked to him or to Seseljevci from Serbia. The evidence actually shows the participation of Blagojevic and his Seseljevci in the take-over and the torturing of detainees in Luka camp by Blagojevic's unit. The implementation of the common purpose in Bijeljina and Bosanski Samac was followed by its implementation in Brcko. Some detainees in camps in Samac were subjected to the patterns of the JCE in all three municipalities: Arrested and detained in Samac, then transferred to Brcko, and transferred again to Bijeljina when the conflict reached Brcko. In sum, municipalities throughout Bosnia and Croatia were subjected to discriminatory, illegal arming, the arrival of the Seseljevci units and other paramilitaries, Serb take-overs of power and crimes. These patterns of implementation of the JCE which began in Croatia continued in the Bosnian crime-base municipalities. My colleague Ms. Iodice will now discuss the first two of those municipalities and explain the implementation of the JCE members' common purpose in Zvornik and in Greater Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Madam. You have the floor for the rest of the presentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning. The crimes committed in Zvornik were in furtherance of the common purpose of the JCE. The evidence proves that on the 8th of April, 1992, Serb forces, including Seseljevci, attacked Zvornik. Over the following months, Serb forces turned the multi-ethnic society of Zvornik into a purely Serb municipality starting by expelling non-Serbs, looting and destroying their property, and culminating in the mistreatment, torture, sexual assault, and murder of hundreds of non-Serbs. The attack on Zvornik was prepared well in advance by members of the Serb municipal authorities, which were established by the SDS in Zvornik with the support of the DB Serbia, the JNA, and the SDS of BiH. These authorities were controlled by JCE members, including Veljko Kadijevic and Radovan Karadzic. The common purpose of the JCE members was to ethnically cleanse Zvornik of its non-Serb population and create a Serb-controlled area. The attack was carried out by Serb forces, including Seseljevci sent by the accused. The Seseljevci formed part of the hierarchical SRS/SCP structure controlled by the accused and operated in co-operation with or under the command of other Serb forces and municipal authorities, which were under the command and control of other JCE members, including Radovan Karadzic. In his brief, the accused claims that the crimes committed in Zvornik were not part of a common purpose and that no JCE was in existence. The accused ignored the evidence on the record, which proves beyond a reasonable doubt that crimes were committed in furtherance of the common purpose and that the accused is responsible for them. These claims are even contradicted by the admissions of the accused, as it can be seen in an interview he gave before the indictment against him was issued, where he explained how the JCE members had planned the take-over of Zvornik long in advance. This is Exhibit P644, time code 01:05:13 through 01:07:30.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Well, in May 1992, Milosevic finally took absolute control over the Yugoslav People's Army. This is when a new constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was declared and when he formally, actually and inherently became the main person in the state - the man who decides everything. This Zvornik operation too was planned in Belgrade and the Bosnian Serb forces took part in it as they had more manpower. However, the special units and the most militant units came from this side. These were police units, the so-called Red Berets. These were special units of the Serbian State Security Service. They were volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party, Arkan's volunteers and another smaller group of volunteers also under the control of the police. The army was not very involved in this operation. For the most part, it provided artillery support where needed. The operation had been planned long in advance, there had been lengthy preparations for it so there were no anxious calls of 'Hurry-up, we need this or that urgently!' Everything was well organised and carried out until the hostilities ended. Later, when looting began, no one was able to control it. "LS: Whose idea was it and how well was it prepared? "VS: This was thought up by key persons from the State Security Service, including Franko Simatovic, Frenki, and he was one of the persons who carried it out. There was some other people too, but I forgot their names. Our volunteers gathered in Loznica, which was their focal point from where they headed to Zvornik. They were led by Vojvoda Cvetinovic and he received orders directly from the special unit commanders."

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Zvornik is located in Eastern BiH on the banks of the Drina River, demarcating the border with Serbia. Zvornik had a number of bridges, main roads, and a railroad connecting Serbia with Serb-populated areas further west in BiH. Because of the strategic location, the municipality of Zvornik was important for the creation of a Serb-dominated area. The take-over of Zvornik realised three of the strategic goals of the 12th of May, 1992, discussed in Exhibit P966. Strategic goal number 1, the separation of the Serb people from the two other national communities. Strategic goal number 2, the establishment of a corridor of Serb-controlled land spanning from Serbia through Bosnia-Herzegovina to Serbian Krajina. Strategic goal number 3, the elimination of the Drina River border between Serbia and Republika Srpska. The local Serb leadership followed the policies of their leaders in BiH to implement the common purpose in Zvornik. First, at least by October 1991 Crisis Staffs were set up. Second, the local Serb leadership established separate municipal authorities and a Serb police force pursuant to the Variant A and B instructions. Variant B was implemented in December 1991, when the SDS established the Serb municipality of Zvornik, and Jovo Mijatovic, who openly spoke of the plan to exchange populations to create mono-ethnic areas, was chosen as its president. Third, the Bosnian Serb leadership monitored the implementation of its policy decisions in Zvornik. As a representative of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, Mijatovic was in contact with the SDS Crisis Staff at the level of BiH and with JCE members Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, and Biljana Plavsic. But updates also came from the SDS in Zvornik, as it kept the SDS leadership informed of its progress in the implementation of the instructions in the municipality. At the same time, the Serb authorities started military preparations for the implementation of the common purpose, assisted by the leadership of the DB Serbia, under the control of JCE member Jovica Stanisic, and in co-operation with other institutions under the command and control of other JCE members, including Karadzic's SDS in BiH, Kadijevic's JNA, and the accused's SRS/SCP. For example, in October 1991 the SCP Mali Zvornik, which had frequent contacts with the SRS/SCP in Belgrade, organised a group of volunteers to be sent to Darda in Croatia for military training. At that time, Rade Kostic from the DB Serbia was the head of the police for the area where the training was held. After the adoption of the Variant A and B instructions DB Serbia, the JNA, the TO, and the SDS intensified the provision of weapons to local Serbs in Zvornik. For example, between December 1991 and March 1992, the DB Serbia provided weapons to Zvornik from Croatia through Rade Kostic and Marko Pavlovic and with the assistance of JCE member Radmilo Bogdanovic. Bogdanovic, assisted by Kostic, also provided weapons from Belgrade after meeting with the SDS leaders of Zvornik. The involvement of DB Serbia in the arming and training of Serbs in Zvornik is shown by this slide and is based on Exhibits P1039, P1144, P1029, P1028, P1027, P1077, P1085, and the testimony of VS-037. As we can see, Pavlovic referred to Kostic as his boss while Kostic was subordinated to Milan Tepavcevic, who was Jovica Stanisic's deputy. Tepavcevic was responsible for the Zvornik military operations and met regularly with the local police commander who co-operated with Bogdanovic and Kostic to obtain weapons. Also the Zvornik MUP started arming Serbs by handing out weapons licences in an uncontrolled way, while other Serbs received weapons through the police or JNA reserve forces. Since the Muslims of Zvornik were dismissed from the JNA reserve forces, the distribution of weapons to JNA reservists meant arming only Serbs. Once parallel political and military structures were in place, the local Serb leadership in Zvornik finalised the preparations for the take-over by arranging the deployment of Seseljevci to Zvornik and the move of Arkan and his men from Bijeljina to Zvornik. The Serb municipality of Zvornik requested volunteers from the SRS/SCP a few days before the take-over. Shortly after, Witness Rankic and another member of the SRS War Staff, together with Vojin Vuckovic, aka Zuca, and his brother Dusan, aka Repic, met with representatives of the Serb municipality in Mali Zvornik to discuss the deployment of the Seseljevci. They agreed that the Seseljevci were going to be equipped, armed, and incorporated in the TO, but would remain together as a unit and were going to be lodged at the Karakaj shoe factory in Karakaj -- at the Standard shoe factory in Karakaj. The accused approved the deployment of Seseljevci to Zvornik and admitted, in Exhibit P1233, that he had a high control -- a high degree of control over them. Two days later, a group of Seseljevci under the command of Vojin Vuckovic, aka Zuca, arrived in Karakaj. This is confirmed by victims detained at the Standard shoe factory and is shown in Exhibit P305, which should not be broadcast. This is a sketch of the Standard shoe factory prepared by Witness VS-1013, whose evidence will be discussed later on, showing that Seseljevci, under number 1, were in fact lodged at the Standard shoe factory. Seseljevci and other members of the Serb forces committed crimes in Zvornik. In his brief, the accused claims that the crimes alleged in the indictment have not been proven and that he is not linked to any of the perpetrators. The accused also claims that his Seseljevci withdrew from Zvornik after the fall of Kula Grad. The accused's claims are contrary to the evidence on the record and should be rejected. For the detailed identification of the groups of Seseljevci that took part in the take-over of Zvornik and their link to the accused, I refer back to paragraphs 291 through 298 of the Prosecution's closing brief, and I will now highlight the evidence proving that Seseljevci linked to the accused perpetrated crimes in Zvornik. The evidence proves beyond a reasonable doubt - and the accused does not contest - that Seseljevci participated in the attack on Zvornik. Together with Arkan's men, the Seseljevci forcibly displaced and murdered non-Serbs. The JNA forces under Tacic's command provided artillery support during the attack. On the 5th of April, 1992, Radio Zvornik announced to the inhabitants of Zvornik town to take shelter for their own safety. VS-1062, her husband and two sons, and their neighbours took shelter in the basement of the building where she lived. They were all unarmed non-Serb civilians. On or about the 9th of April, 1992, a group of Arkan's men stormed into the shelter and forced all the men out. A group of Seseljevci entered the shelter and took the women and children away, while the men were lined up against the wall. VS-1062 heard gun-fire from the location where the men were standing. VS-1062's husband and sons and all the others were never seen again. They were executed by Arkan's men. VS-1062 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the sake of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: VS-1062 and the other women and children were put on a bus and deported to Serbia. The testimony of VS-1062 is clear. Arkan's men and Seseljevci co-operated to murder able-bodied non-Serb men and to expel women and children from Zvornik. VS-1062 explained to the Court how, first, Arkan's men burst into the shelter and took all the men out; then a different group, who introduced themselves as Seseljevci and wore different uniforms, escorted the women and children away while Arkan's men executed the men. VS-1062 also explained the pattern followed by Arkan's men and Seseljevci at transcript 5958. Quote: "These men were going from house to house, from door to door, killing men." The success of this pattern was recorded by JCE member Mladic in his diary, Exhibit P1347, when, briefed by Marko Pavlovic, he noted that volunteer formations "led by Arkan and Seselj" "enjoyed exceptional success." The accused claims that VS-1062 did not mention Seseljevci in a statement given to the BiH authorities in 2003. This claim is baseless and should be dismissed. VS-1062 denied that the 2003 statement to the BiH authorities which is not in evidence is hers. She denied ever having contacts with the authorities of BiH and ever living at the address indicated on that statement. VS-1062 also did not recognise the signature. These crimes and Seseljevci's participation have been proven beyond a reasonable doubt. Even though the accused is contesting the participation of Seseljevci in the murder, he admits, for example, at transcript 1933, that Seseljevci participated in the attack together with other Serb forces. The accused admitted that the SRS municipal committee in Loznica organised a group of Seseljevci for the take-over of Zvornik and one of the Seseljevci guarding VS-1062 and the other non-Serbs before they were forcibly displaced stated that he hailed from Loznica. The evidence of VS-1062, VS-1013, VS-038, Boskovic, Jovic, and VS-1087 proves beyond a reasonable doubt that as a result of the attack by the Serb forces, which included Seseljevci, non-Serbs fled out of fear or were rounded up and deported to Serbia and many of them were killed. Your Honours, would this be a good place to stop?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you continue for another seven minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Of course. After the fall of Kula Grad on the 26th of April, 1992, non-Serbs who had remained hiding in Zvornik were arrested as they tried to flee towards Muslim territory and taken to the detention facilities as in the case of Witnesses VS-1013, VS-1015, and Fadil Kopic, or were arrested in their homes as in the case of VS-1063. These witnesses were taken to the detention sites at the Standard shoe factory and Ekonomija farm and later on were transferred to the Ciglane factory. During the detention at these sites, they were brutally abused, tortured, and murdered by members of the Serb forces, as specified in paragraphs 316 through 330 of the Prosecution's closing brief. Amongst the perpetrators the victims identified the Seseljevci from Kraljevo, including Vojvoda Cele, Miroslav Vukovic; Major Toro; Pufta; and Sava; the Seseljevci from Loznica; the Yellow Wasps, including Vojin Vuckovic, aka Zuco, and his brother Dusan Vuckovic, aka Repic; and Pivarski's men, including Stojan Pivarski and Zoks. These groups are linked to the accused and operated in co-operation with or under the command of other Serb forces and municipal authorities which were under the command and control of other JCE members, including Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic. After the take-over, the volunteer units were incorporated into the Serb police and TO, later VRS. The Loznica's group was incorporated into the police. Zuco's Yellow Wasps, Pivarski's men, and others were incorporated into the TO/VRS. The volunteers were housed and paid by the Serb TO and by the Serb municipal authorities. The victims' identification of their abusers has been established beyond a reasonable doubt. The victims spent long periods of time in detention. They learned personal details of their attackers. They saw them day after day. They learned what unit they belonged to directly from them, as VS-1015 also explained at transcript 5406. Witnesses VS-1013, VS-1015, Kopic, and VS-1063 all suffered and witnessed severe abuses by the Seseljevci from Kraljevo and Loznica over an extended period of time. At Ekonomija farm, for example, VS-1063 saw a group of Seseljevci take out a detainee. They shot the detainee in the legs. They carved a cross into his flesh and broke his arm before taking him back into the room, where they stabbed him and shot him to death. At Ciglane, both Kopic and VS-1015 testified that Pufta cut off Cirak's ear and stabbed him. On that same day, Pufta and Sasa then drove Cirak away and shot him to death. On that same day, Pufta, together with Sasa, cut a crescent tattoo off Enver Dautovic's arm with a knife. Sasa then congratulated Dautovic, saying: "You fared well, but if you had been yelling louder you would have ended up with Cirak ..." And this can be found at transcript 5435. The crimes committed at these detention facilities were so grave and gruesome that the witnesses could never forget what they saw and will always remember the perpetrators. VS-1013 observed his abusers for almost three months, from his arrest and transfer to the detention centre at the Standard shoe factory to the day of his transfer from the detention centre at Ciglane factory to the Batkovic camp. While cleaning the premises at the Standard shoe factory, VS-1013 read the names of the groups of Serb forces on the doors of the rooms where they were lodged, including the Seseljevci from Kraljevo, the Loznica group, and military police. Amongst the Seseljevci from Kraljevo, VS-1013 recognised Cele whom the prisoners had to address as Vojvoda and whom the accused held in high esteem. VS-1013 stated at transcript 5210 how the prisoners were told: "A special man will come by. He will talk to you. You mustn't look him in the eyes and you must address him with Vojvoda, sir, honourable Vojvoda sir." Vojvoda Miroslav Vukovic, aka Cele, is not the only Seseljevac identified by VS-1013. For example, VS-1013 saw Major Toro's SRS identification card and in June 1992 heard that Seselj had promoted Sava, Zoks, and Pufta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to stop now because the Judges need to go into the room downstairs for a swearing-in ceremony. We shall return towards ten to 1.00 or so. This is not something in our control. This is our last break for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Madam Prosecutor, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Before we broke, I was describing the evidence of VS-1013, who testified that the detainees were told that the Vojvoda would visit them. The evidence of VS-1013 is credible and reliable, despite the accused's allegations. VS-1013 explained to the Court that he did not explicitly mention Seseljevci in his 1993 statement to the authorities of BiH, but he mentioned the same people, the same nicknames. Later, when he gave a statement to the ICTY in 1996, which, as he said at transcript 5303, was the only official statement he gave, he did his best to recollect every detail. Other witnesses also recognised the same perpetrators as members of the Seseljevci. For example, Witness Kopic who spent almost three months in detention in Zvornik recalled that some members of the Kraljevo group, and Zoks, glorified Seselj as their leader. VS-1015 observed and identified members of the Seseljevci throughout the almost three months he spent in detention, from his arrest on the 7th of May, 1992, to his transfer to Bijeljina in mid-July 1992. While detained at Ciglane factory, VS-1015 was regularly forced to loot by the Seseljevci. VS-1015 recognised Zoks and a man addressed as Vojvoda as those who beat him and beat Nesib Dautovic to death at Ekonomija farm. The evidence demonstrates that the person identified by VS-1015 as Vojvoda is Miroslav Vukovic, aka Cele. The accused has claimed that the man referred to as Vojvoda was instead Dusan Vuckovic, aka Repic. This claim should be rejected. The accused confronted VS-1015 with a 1993 statement given to the BiH authorities, where VS-1015 referred to the Vojvoda he identified as the man present at the beating and murder as Vojvoda Repic. VS-1015 explained to the Court that he never heard anyone refer to the man he identified as Vojvoda with the nickname or surname of Repic and he might have used this nickname by mistake. And I refer the Trial Chamber to transcript 5458. VS-1015 carefully described the man he addressed as Vojvoda. He recalled that Vojvoda had a beard. He recalled that Vojvoda wore some sort of trainers, as he said at transcript 5413, the sort of shoes that elderly women usually wear. These same details are confirmed by VS-027, who recalled, at page 114 of Exhibit P868 and transcript 14607, that Cele wore some sort of women's trainers. The accused himself admitted that Cele limped at transcript 5359. It has been established beyond a reasonable doubt that the man participating in the beatings and murder at Ekonomija farm together with Zoks was Miroslav Vukovic, aka Cele. The accused, in his brief, has also admitted that Cele was in Zvornik until the 17th of May, 1992, confirming his opportunity to take part in the murder of Nesib Dautovic which occurred on or about the 12th of May, 1992. The accused also disputes VS-1015's identification of Seseljevci, claiming that VS-1015 did not mention their affiliation in his 1993 statement to the BiH authorities. VS-1015 explained to the Court that he heard members of the Serb forces refer to the Kraljevo group as Seseljevci. And he also explained that his 1993 statement was given in haste and it is only two pages long, while he gave a much more detailed statement later on to the ICTY. For these reasons, the evidence proves beyond a reasonable doubt that the crimes charged at the Standard shoe factory, Ekonomija farm, and Ciglane factory were committed by the Serb forces, including Seseljevci. Once Zvornik town was cleansed of its non-Serb population, Serb forces started displacing all non-Serbs from settlements around the town, as detailed in paragraphs 302 through 309 of the Prosecution's closing brief. Systematically, between the end of May and the end of June, 1992, non-Serbs were forced out of their homes at short notice. Able-bodied men were separated and forced to detention facilities, where they were severely mistreated, abused, and murdered because of their ethnicity by members of the Serb forces, including Seseljevci. By August 1992, Zvornik and most of the towns along the Drina River had been ethnically cleansed in furtherance of the common purpose. In May 1993, the accused admitted, in Exhibit P1218, how Zvornik, "where many Muslims used to live, is now flooded with Serbs." As Mr. Marcussen had already described in detail, the non-Serb population of Drinjaca-Kostjerevo was amongst those who were forcibly displaced from Zvornik municipality at the end of May 1992. Your Honours heard that women and children were displaced while the men were detained at the Drinjaca Dom Kulture, where they were brutally beaten and murdered. Witness VS-1064 identified the perpetrators of the murder from their uniforms and called them Chetniks, explaining that by "Chetniks" he meant Seseljevci. He repeated at transcript 8738 to 8739: "That's how I view Chetniks, how I see them. Now, if there's someone else, another Chetnik Vojvoda, for instance, who had special insignia ... then I wouldn't say that they were Seselj's men. I would say that they belonged to this other man. But we know of no other man who was involved in this or meddled in Vojislav Seselj's business. Now that there are Chetniks in Croatia, Bosnia, Serbia, and all over the place, we know of only one boss, one head." The identification of these perpetrators as members of the Seseljevci has been proven beyond a reasonable doubt. The non-Serb population of Setici, Djulici, and other neighbouring villages suffered the same fate. After being forced out of their homes by Serb forces, including VRS, police, and paramilitaries, women and children were expelled while the non-Serb men were separated and taken to the detention facility in Karakaj technical school. After being detained for a few days, all non-Serb detainees, approximately 740, were executed. Some were murdered at the Karakaj technical school, some at Gero's slaughter-house. Some of the perpetrators of this crime, namely, the Yellow Wasps, Pivarski's men, and the Loznica's group, formed part of the hierarchical SRS/SCP structure controlled by the accused, as just discussed. The Yellow Wasps, like other paramilitaries in Zvornik, were arrested in July 1992 as they had started looting Serb property as well. They were shortly after released and redeployed. The accused has on several occasions sought to distance himself from the Yellow Wasps. And as the serious crimes committed by them were soon publicly known, the accused denied any affiliation to them to avoid political liability, as Witness Rankic stated in Exhibit P1074. However, when the head of the TO, Marko Pavlovic, had complaints about the Yellow Wasps' behaviour, he directed them to the SRS/SCP in Belgrade and the accused responded to these complaints by redeploying the Yellow Wasps to Skelani instead of calling them back to Serbia or dismissing them. Pivarski's men were also a group of Seseljevci. Its commander, Stojan Pivarski, held the rank of major in the SCP, while his deputy Ivan Korac, aka Zoks, held the rank of captain. And if we could now move shortly in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You really have to move to private session? Can't you do it otherwise? Because normally in closing arguments I like it to be public. Okay, let's move to private session and we'll see whether we should lift the confidentiality of it later on or not. Please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: The accused has claimed, based on a list of members

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: (redacted) VS-038's membership to either group is anyway irrelevant. The evidence proves that these groups worked together and eventually were arrested together. We can now move back to open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: The Loznica group was also linked to the accused and, as stated above, the accused admits that the SRS municipal committee in Loznica organised a group of Seseljevci for the take-over of Zvornik. The link of Yellow Wasps, Pivarski's men, and Loznica's group to the accused is proven beyond a reasonable doubt by Witnesses Rankic and Jovic, whose evidence is corroborated by Witnesses Drazilovic, VS-027, Alic, VS-036, VS-038, and Exhibit P971. Crimes of the same nature were also committed at Celopek Dom Kulture, where non-Serb men were transferred after being expelled from their homes in Divic by members of the army and police, following the same well-established pattern. VS-1065 detailed in his evidence the severe mistreatment, sexual assault, torture, and murder to which the inmates at Celopek were subjected. He identified the perpetrators as Dusan Vuckovic, aka Repic; Major Toro; Pufta; and Zoks. For example, on one occasion Repic selected some prisoners and carved crosses on their forehead with a knife. On Bajram day, a Muslim holiday, Repic returned to Celopek Dom Kulture, selected fathers and sons amongst the detainees, ordered them onto a stage, and forced them to engage in oral sex. He then started shooting at the detainees on the stage and killing them. The accused did not contest VS-1065's evidence. He stated that VS-1065 testified truthfully. As shown above and detailed in paragraph 291 of the Prosecution's closing brief, these perpetrators were linked to the accused. After the displacement of non-Serbs from Divic, it was Kozluk's turn to be cleansed. Initially, Muslims in Kozluk were allowed to stay in their homes. However, non-Serbs were intimidated, abused, and killed by the Serb forces which occupied the town. Those forces included men under the command of Marko Pavlovic, Zoran Subotic, Arkan, Pivarski, Zuco, Niski, and Captain Dragan. Despite having complied with the order of handing over their weapons, on the 26th of June, 1992, the Muslims were forced onto buses and trucks and deported to Serbia. Those who refused were killed. The Serb forces that carried out the displacement included members of the army, police, TO, Arkan's men, and Yellow Wasps. With the cleansing of the last non-Serb villages, the implementation of the common purpose in Zvornik had entered its final stage. Exhibit P1347 proves how a few days after the deportation of the non-Serbs from Kozluk on the 30th of June, 1992, Branko Grujic announced to JCE members Ratko Mladic and Radovan Karadzic that the Zvornik Serb leadership had "successfully implemented the President's," Karadzic, "decision to settle Divic and Kozluk with our children." "Our children," namely Serbs. That the crimes committed in Zvornik were part of the JCE common purpose is also evidenced by the large-scale destruction of mosques and religious institutions carried out by the Serb forces after the take-over of Zvornik, as detailed in paragraphs 345 through 348 of the Prosecution's closing brief. A few examples demonstrate that the intent behind the destruction of Muslim religious property was to erase the existence of Zvornik's Muslim population. In Divic, the historic Dervis lodge was destroyed and a junked lorry was placed on the top of the graves of two Muslim saints. An Orthodox church replaced the Divic mosque. The sites of the destroyed Rijecanska mosque and Begsuja mosque in Zvornik and the mosque of Mehmed-Celebi in Kozluk were used as rubbish dumps. The destruction was carried out by the Serb TO because they were symbols of the Muslim culture and not for military purposes, as testified by VS-037 and VS-038. To conclude, the evidence discussed proves beyond a reasonable doubt that the crimes charged in relation to the municipality of Zvornik were committed by members of the Serb forces, including Seseljevci. These crimes were an integral part of the common purpose to ethnically cleanse Serb-targeted territories in BiH of its non-Serb population and create a Serb-controlled area. I will now turn to the Greater Sarajevo area. The crimes committed in Greater Sarajevo were part of the common purpose. The evidence proves beyond a reasonable doubt that a JCE was in place and that its common purpose included the take-overs of Ilijas, Vogosca, Novo Sarajevo, and Ilidza, and the resulting crimes committed by members of the Serb forces, including Seseljevci. The Seseljevci formed part of the hierarchical SRS/SCP structure controlled by the accused and, as in Zvornik, operated in co-operation with or under the command of other Serb forces and municipal authorities, such as the JNA, TO, and later VRS and MUP, which were under the command and control of JCE members, including Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic. The accused claims that the crimes committed in Greater Sarajevo were not part of the common purpose and that no JCE was in existence. These crimes should be rejected. I'm sorry, Your Honours, I meant these claims should be rejected. Sarajevo was a key location in the pursuit of the common purpose. At the 8th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly in February 1992, JCE member Karadzic explained the importance of Sarajevo, saying, quote: "Leaving Sarajevo, where there are 215.000 Serbs including Yugoslavs, where there are great riches, if we left Sarajevo, well, we should be hanged," and this is found in Exhibit P949. Karadzic's position was reflected in the strategic objectives of the Serb people in BiH on the 12th of May, 1992, Exhibit P966, when the establishment of Serb control in and around Sarajevo was deemed essential to the achievement of the first and fifth of the strategic objectives, namely, the separation of Serbs from Croats and Muslims and the division of Sarajevo into Serb and Muslim parts. The accused has attempted to distance himself from the SRS in BiH and from the Vojvodas active in the Greater Sarajevo area. His claims are contrary to the evidence and should be dismissed. The accused has admitted in Exhibit P199 [sic] that at least from May 1992, the SRS had a branch in BiH, and he has stated in Exhibit P1219 that the SRS was "the second political party in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." The accused has also admitted, in Exhibit P1215, having "a considerable number of volunteers" in Sarajevo. This is confirmed by other evidence on the record, for example, Exhibits C10 and P836, proving that significant numbers of Seseljevci were sent to Ilijas, Vogosca, Ilidza, and the Jewish cemetery near Grbavica throughout the war. The Vojvodas present in Greater Sarajevo came from that area and the accused has confirmed his link to them before the indictment against him was issued. He stated in Exhibit P644, page 14, quote: "Grbavica was saved by our volunteers, mainly by Vojvoda Slavko Aleksic. You've heard of Slavko Aleksic. He's still at the Jewish cemetery. He is our member of the central homeland administration, the highest party leadership, and he's been there since the first day of the war. What he managed to save stayed Serbian and no one else could take it. There was also Vojvoda Branislav Gavrilovic, aka Brne, and Vojvoda Vasko in Ilijas." In furtherance of the common purpose, Serb leaders in Greater Sarajevo started implementation of the Variant A and B instructions, creating Crisis Staffs and Serb-only Municipal Assemblies. The implementation of the instructions in Novo Sarajevo was confirmed by Vojvoda Slavko Aleksic in Exhibit P1102. Aleksic at the same time had an important role in both the SRS and the SDS. Similarly, in Ilidza, the proclamation of the Serb Assembly on the 3rd of January, 1992, was in accordance with the SDS Main Board instructions of the 19th of December, 1991. On the 24th of March, 1992, the creation of the Serb municipalities of Vogosca and Rajlovac was announced at the 12th Session of the Assembly of the Serb people in BiH. Finally, right before the outbreak of the conflict, the Ilijas SDS separated the municipality from the district of Sarajevo and annexed it to the so-called Serb Autonomous District of Romanija. Like in other parts of BiH, Serb leaders started military preparations in Greater Sarajevo, in furtherance of the common purpose. While in October 1991, the council of the SDS was discussing the need to start military preparations, JCE member Karadzic, referring to the impending war in Sarajevo and the prospect of the disappearance of the Muslim people "from the face of the earth," stated that "there are 20.000 armed Serbs around Sarajevo," and this can be found in Exhibit P502, page 7. A Serb police force was set up throughout Greater Sarajevo. Shortly after the 3rd of April, 1992, the Novo Sarajevo MUP formed a Serb MUP station at Vraca. In Ilidza, just prior to the outbreak of the war, the head of the Ilidza special police disbanded the existing ethnically mixed reserve police force and set it up again with only Serb policemen [sic]. In Ilijas, Serb policemen assisted by Serb policemen from other municipalities took control of the police station. The SRS significantly contributed to the military preparations in Greater Sarajevo. In Exhibit P1319, Vojvoda Slavko Aleksic stated that although the election of Alija Izetbegovic made it difficult for Serbs to arm themselves, he did his best to ensure Serbs in Novo Sarajevo did not fall behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Let's move back into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. IODICE
utterances.text: Going back to the SRS contribution to the military preparation in Greater Sarajevo, Branislav Gavrilovic, aka Brne, explained, in Exhibit P1000, how, upon his return to Greater Sarajevo, his Seseljevci were armed by Major Krstovic, commander of the Sarajevo city defence. Brne also admitted, in Exhibit P999, capturing the TO warehouse in Ilidza where 50.000 weapons were located, bragged about disarming Muslims, and explained how these weapons "contributed to the defence of all Serb people from Sarajevo jihad fighters." Brne's statement mirrors the accused's efforts to associate Bosnian Muslims with Islamist fundamentalists. Nikola Poplasen also played an important role organising and arming Serbs in BiH. The accused admitted this in Exhibit P218, when he promoted Poplasen to Vojvoda in March 1994. The efforts of the Serb leaders to prepare militarily for the implementation of the common purpose can be summarised in the words of the Ilijas deputy to the Assembly of the Serb people in BiH, who less than a month before the attack by Serb forces on Ljesevo confirmed Serbs in Ilijas were prepared for war in Exhibit P966. "We are organised and I have asked the TV to come and record how well organised for the war we in Ilijas are, how our defence lines are organised. It is true, yes, that we have stolen a lot of goods. We have a lot of provisions down there to live on ... we have cut off and mined the railway line and no one can now get into Sarajevo. We have mined the motorway too. We shall do our best to prevent the enemy from ever getting to Sarajevo from the direction of Zenica, and anyone who tries the upper route will also meet his end." Serb forces, including Seseljevci, committed crimes in Greater Sarajevo. As in other areas of BiH, once parallel political and military structures were set up, Serb forces, including Seseljevci, attacked and took control of the municipalities. The evidence proves beyond a reasonable doubt that in the course of and following the take-overs in Greater Sarajevo, non-Serbs were expelled, killed, detained or put under house arrest, mistreated, and otherwise persecuted. Detainees were subjected to forced labour in dangerous conditions at the front lines, where on multiple occasions they were used as human shields. Non-Serb property and cultural monuments were systematically plundered and/or destroyed. In his brief, the accused claims that the crimes alleged in the indictment have not been proven and that he is not linked to any of the perpetrators. These claims are contrary to the evidence on the record and should be rejected. For the deployment of Seseljevci to the Greater Sarajevo area and for the identification of the Vojvodas fighting with their Seseljevci in the area and the link to the accused, I refer back to paragraphs 255 through 263 and 358 through 375 of the Prosecution's closing brief. I will now highlight the evidence proving beyond a reasonable doubt that Seseljevci perpetrated crimes in Greater Sarajevo and that these perpetrators were linked to the accused. The evidence of Witnesses VS-1111, VS-1055, Mujo Dzafic, and Exhibit P451 proves that the attack on Ljesevo was carried out by the VRS, members of the Ilijas TO, and by a group of Seseljevci led by Vojvoda Vasilije Vidovic, aka Vaske. Contrary to the accused's claims, it has been proven beyond a reasonable doubt that Vasilije Vidovic, aka Vaske, and his Seseljevci took part in the attack on Ljesevo together with members of the Ilijas TO, resulting in the forcible displacement of the non-Serb population and the murder of 22 non-Serbs. VS-1055 explained how in the afternoon on the 5th of June, 1992, he recognised Seseljevac Vaske and TO member Ranko Draskic amongst the members of the Serb forces that captured him. He saw Amir Fazlic falling to the ground, shot in the head, when Vaske approached him with one of his Seseljevci. Earlier that day, while the shelling was still ongoing, Ranko Draskic had taken part with other TO members in the murder of another 21 non-Serbs. The accused claims that VS-1055 did not mention Vaske's presence in his 1992 statement to the BiH authorities. VS-1055 explained that his 1992 statement was given immediately after the trauma he had experienced and with time he remembered more details. In any event, the accused has admitted in Exhibit P644 the presence of his commander Vaske at the Ilijas front. It has been established beyond a reasonable doubt that Vaske was amongst the Serb forces that took over Ljesevo and murdered non-Serbs. In April 1992, in Svrake, Vogosca, Serb forces including the special unit led by Rajko Jankovic, attacked the village, rounded up its non-Serb population, displaced women, elderly, and children, while detaining able-bodied men. The implementation of the common purpose was so successful that JCE member Ratko Mladic noted in his diary, on the 6th of June, 1992, that there were "no more houses or inhabitants in Svrake," and this can be found in Exhibit P1346. Would this be a good moment to stop, Your Honours?
